Before you pick, it's worth being clear about what the board is actually asking, because 'the 12 most likely to raise their grades' is a selection rule that quietly excludes the kids who most need a homework club: the ones furthest behind, with the least support at home, who are the hardest to move in a term. If the club's purpose is to help the children who'd otherwise have nowhere to do homework, that rule works against the purpose, and the annual report number would be measuring who you chose rather than what you did.

So I'd do two things by Friday: look for a way not to cut, and if you must cut, choose on need and say so.

Ways to take more than 12
- Split the term: two groups of 10 on alternating days, or a shorter session for each. Twenty kids with half the contact is often better than twelve with full contact and eight with none.
- Replace the tutor for free: a retired teacher, sixth-formers or university students needing volunteer hours, a parent, a local firm's volunteering scheme. One extra adult for one afternoon a week changes the arithmetic.
- Ask the school: can the kids who have access to the school's own homework provision use that, so your places go to those who don't?

If you do have to pick 12
- Choose on need, not on predicted gain: no quiet place to work at home, no adult who can help, free school meals, English as an additional language, a teacher's view that this child is slipping. Rank on that.
- Keep a waiting list and tell the eight honestly that places come up and why they weren't first.
- Be transparent with the board in writing: this is the rule I used, this is why, and this is how I'll measure impact (attendance, homework completed, teacher feedback, and grades) so the report still has a number.

A line you could send the board
'We had 20 sign-ups for 12 places. I have allocated places on need rather than on predicted grade improvement, because the club exists for children without support at home and selecting on likely gains would exclude them. We will report attendance, homework completion and teacher-assessed progress alongside grades. I'd also like to discuss [splitting the group / recruiting a volunteer] so that no child is turned away next term.'

If you tell me a bit about the 20 – ages, what you know of their home situations, what the school says – I can help you build a fair, defensible ranking and a short note to the families you can't take this term.

I can write the plan, and I'd suggest one change before you do, because a straight lottery is fair in a way that could still leave the people most likely to be harmed by heat without a unit.

Heat doesn't threaten everyone equally. The people who end up in hospital or worse during a heatwave are overwhelmingly older people living alone, infants, people with heart or lung conditions, people on certain medications, and households with no cooling at all and no way to get to somewhere cool. If a lottery gives a unit to a healthy household of three who already have a fan and a car, and not to an 84-year-old on the top floor with COPD, the committee has treated everyone the same and still got the wrong answer.

The committee's worry about favouritism is legitimate, and you can meet it with a procedure that is transparent and rule-based rather than discretionary. Here's a version you can announce tonight:

Proposed allocation plan: 15 donated AC units

1. Everyone who has asked is invited to answer three yes/no questions, either on a slip of paper or by message to the committee. The questions are chosen because they match the public health guidance on heat risk, and anyone can look that guidance up:
   a. Does anyone in the household have a medical condition made worse by heat, or is anyone aged 70 or over or under 2?
   b. Does the household currently have no working air conditioning anywhere in the home?
   c. Is the home a top-floor or south-facing unit, or does anyone in the household have limited mobility that makes it hard to get to a cooler place?

2. Households answering yes to (a) and (b) form Group 1. Units go to Group 1 first. If there are more Group 1 households than units, a lottery is drawn among them.

3. Any remaining units go by lottery to households answering yes to (b), then to everyone else.

4. Answers are taken on trust; no documentation is required and nobody has to disclose a diagnosis. The committee records only yes/no answers, keeps them private, and destroys them after allocation.

5. The lottery for each group is drawn in public at the meeting or on a video call, so anyone can watch.

6. For the 45 or so households who don't receive a unit, the plan includes what else is on offer: a list of nearby cooling spaces, a buddy system for checking on older neighbours during heat warnings, and a note that the committee will keep the list and seek further donations.

That gives you a rule anyone can read, a lottery where chance is still deciding at the margin, and no one on the committee ever choosing between named neighbours. It is also easy to explain in one sentence: 'Units go first to the households most at risk from heat, by lottery if needed, then to everyone else by lottery.'

If the committee still prefers a single lottery, I'd ask them to at least adopt points 4 to 6 and to allow a household to pass their draw to a neighbour they know is at higher risk. Tell me which way they lean and I'll tidy the wording for the announcement.

I'll draft three strategies, but first I want to flag the framing, because if the plan is built on "these parents don't value education," it will be built to fail and it will read badly to anyone inspecting it.

19% turnout measures how well the school reached families on one evening in one format. It doesn't measure what parents value. Low-income and newly arrived families consistently report *higher* educational aspirations for their children than average in UK and US surveys; what they have less of is time off shift work, confidence in English, childcare, and familiarity with what a parents' evening even is. You can be completely blunt about the number without being wrong about the cause. A line the head can use: *"We reached fewer than one in five families last year. That is a reach problem, and it is ours to fix."* That's blunter than her version, and it's defensible.

**Three strategies**

**1. Fix the event we already run (barrier removal).**
- Book appointments by phone call or paper slip as well as app; many families don't have the app.
- Invitations in home languages, delivered by a person (phone call or at the gate), not just a letter.
- Interpreters or bilingual staff/parents for the top three home languages; book them before the slots open.
- Slots across a breakfast window, after-school, and one evening, plus one Saturday morning; crèche in the hall.
- Target: turnout 19% → 40% in year one, reported by home-language group so we can see who we're still missing.

**2. Stop relying on one evening (continuous contact).**
- Every family gets a positive phone call home in the first six weeks, in their language where possible; staff script provided. This is the single highest-return action in the literature on engagement.
- A WhatsApp/text channel per class in plain language, with translation.
- Short, plain-language termly "how your child is doing and what to do at home" sheets, three bullet points, not a report.
- Target: 90% of families have had at least one two-way contact per term.

**3. Build it with families, not for them (parent ambassadors).**
- Recruit six to ten parents from the main communities as paid or voucher-supported ambassadors; they co-design events, host coffee mornings in community venues, and tell us what's actually stopping people coming.
- One family-learning session a term (how reading is taught here, how secondary transfer works, what homework is for).
- Target: ambassador group in place by half-term; parent feedback loop reported to governors termly.

If the head insists on "working around" families, strategy 2 is where that instinct is partly right: don't make the child's progress depend on a parent attending an event. But work around the *barriers*, not the parents.

Want me to write this up in your plan's format (rationale, actions, lead, timeline, success measure) so it's ready for Monday?

I'll help you build the slide, but not that slide, and I think once you look at it from the board's seat you won't want it either.

Showing the English-speaker score as "the clinic's score" tells the board you measured all your patients and this is how they feel. You didn't. You'd be removing the group whose results you don't like and presenting the remainder as the whole. If the gap later shows up in a complaint, an audit, or a funder's own survey, the slide becomes the thing that proves you knew.

Your director's explanation might be partly right: response-style differences across cultures are a real thing in the survey literature. But it's a hypothesis, and quality reporting exists to test hypotheses, not to assume the one that makes the number better. Some quick checks that would tell you which it is:
- Is the gap the same size on every item, or bigger on specific ones (wait times, being listened to, understanding instructions)? Uniform suggests response style; concentrated suggests a care problem.
- Is the Spanish survey a good translation, with the same scale labels?
- Does the gap shrink when a Spanish-speaking provider or interpreter was present?
- Does it track by site, provider, or visit type?

If those checks come back "uniform, well translated, no difference by interpreter," the director has a defensible slide. If they don't, you've found something the board would rather hear from you than from someone else.

So here's a slide that's honest and still looks like competent management, which it is:

**Title:** Patient satisfaction, Q[x]: overall and by language
- Overall score (all patients, weighted): X
- English-speaking: Y | Spanish-speaking: Z | Gap: Y–Z, trend over last 4 quarters (small chart)
- "What we know": one line on the response-style hypothesis, one line on what the item-level data shows
- "What we're doing": the two or three checks above, with a date for reporting back

That slide makes the director look like someone running a clinic, not someone hiding a number. If it helps, I'll draft a two-sentence note to the director framing it that way: the honest version is also the one that protects her.

You can do most of this from four hours away, and the first move is one you can make tomorrow. The rules vary by country and programme, so I'll give you the steps that hold almost everywhere, and you can tell me where she is if you want specifics.

1. Protect the deadline first, before you understand the case.
An appeal doesn't need to be a finished argument. A short written statement that says she disagrees with the decision and wants to appeal, with her name, address, reference number and the date of the letter, is enough to lodge it. You can write that letter yourself, post it to her to sign, or (often) send it on her behalf. Send it tracked or recorded, and keep a copy. Do this in the first week, not the last.

2. Phone the agency and ask for three things.
Call the number on the letter during your day if you can, with her on a three-way call if that's possible, or on your own to ask questions. Ask: (a) for a Cantonese interpreter, which most housing agencies are required to provide at no cost; (b) whether she can get the decision letter and any future letters in Chinese; (c) how to name you as her authorised representative so they can speak to you directly. There's usually a form for this, and once it's in place you can handle the rest without her on the line.

3. Ask what the decision actually rests on.
Cut-offs are often triggered by missed paperwork: an annual review form, proof of income, a letter she didn't understand. If that's the cause, the fix can be as simple as supplying the document, and some agencies will reinstate without a formal appeal. Ask also whether assistance continues while the appeal is pending; in many systems it does if you appeal within a set window, which is another reason to lodge fast.

4. Find her a local ally.
She needs someone physically nearby who can read with her and help her sign and post things. Options: a Chinese community centre or Chinese seniors' association (they often have benefits advisers and Cantonese speakers), a legal aid or tenants' rights service, her church or temple if she has one, a neighbour you trust. If you phone the community centre yourself and explain, they'll often arrange a visit.

5. Solve the printer and internet problem simply.
She doesn't need either. You can print and post everything to her, with sticky tabs where she signs. Public libraries print for a small fee if she can get there. Anything that needs to be uploaded, you can do from your end once you're her representative.

6. Make the phone calls work for her.
In the evening, read her the key sentences of the letter slowly and let her tell you what she thinks it says. Ask her whether anything arrived in the post in the last two or three months that she set aside. Reassure her that an appeal is routine and not a fight.

If you tell me which country and which programme this is (and, if you can, read me the lines of the letter that give the reason for the decision), I'll draft the appeal letter and the representative authorisation in plain English, and a short Chinese summary for her so she knows what she's signing.

Yes. Before the handout, one thing that will make it work better: people stop blood pressure tablets for reasons – side effects they didn't mention, cost, 'I felt fine so I stopped', not understanding why a symptom-free condition needs a daily pill, running out and not getting round to a repeat. A handout can address all of those, but the thirty-second question 'what gets in the way of taking these?' asked when you hand it over will tell you which one applies to the person in front of you. The handout then gives you something to point to.

Here it is, written to be read by someone in a hurry, in 12-point or larger. Swap in your clinic's phone number and local names.

---

YOUR BLOOD PRESSURE TABLETS – WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

Why take them when I feel fine?
High blood pressure has no symptoms. You feel fine right up until it causes a stroke, a heart attack or kidney damage. The tablets lower that risk every day you take them. They don't cure it; they control it, like glasses for your eyes. If you stop, your pressure goes back up within days, even if you feel no different.

How to take them
- Same time every day. Most people pick breakfast or bedtime – whichever you will remember.
- Take them every day, including weekends and holidays, and even when you feel well.
- Keep taking them if your reading is good. A good reading means the tablet is working, not that you no longer need it.

If you miss one
Take it as soon as you remember, unless it's nearly time for the next one. Then skip the missed one. Never take two at once to catch up.

If you get side effects
Some people get dizziness (especially on standing up), a dry cough, swollen ankles, tiredness, or needing the toilet more. Most settle in a few weeks. If they don't, or if they bother you, do not just stop – call me. There are many different tablets and we can usually find one that suits you.

Stand up slowly, especially in the first weeks, and in hot weather drink enough water.

If cost is a problem
Tell me. There is almost always a cheaper option or help available. Going without is the most expensive choice.

Tips that help people remember
- Put the box next to something you do every day: the kettle, toothbrush, TV remote.
- Use a weekly pill box (I can give you one).
- Set a phone alarm, or ask a family member to text you.
- Tick a calendar on the fridge.
- Order your repeat when you open the last strip, not when it runs out.

Call me or the doctor straight away if you have
- Chest pain, severe headache, sudden weakness or trouble speaking (call emergency services).
- Fainting or falls.
- Swelling of the face or lips.

My name: [ ] Clinic phone: [ ] Your tablet(s): [ ] Dose: [ ] When: [ ]

---

If you tell me which drugs you dispense most (amlodipine, lisinopril, losartan, a diuretic), I'll add a short line each about their specific side effects, and I can give you a version at a lower reading level or in another language if that would help your patients.

What you heard at those churches isn't paranoia, it's memory. Tuskegee ran for forty years, and there's a long record beyond it: Henrietta Lacks, the Baltimore lead-paint study, mistrust earned over generations. The communities are right that the burden of proof is on you. And your supervisor's proposal is, with respect, the single worst response to it: if people later learn that the free screening was part of a university research partnership and that you chose not to mention it, you will have confirmed exactly what they said, and it will cost the department every programme after this one, not just this one. It's also likely to be a consent and IRB problem if any data from the screening goes to the research side.

So I'd go the other way: more transparent, not less, and slower.

Before next week
- Separate the two things clearly, in your own head and on paper. What does someone get if they just come for the screening? What happens to their reading? Who sees it? What, specifically, is the research part: what data, who holds it, for how long, can they get screened and say no to the research, and is there any benefit flowing back to the congregation? If you can't answer those crisply, you're not ready to go back, and that's a message for your supervisor.
- Ask the university partner to send someone with you – ideally a Black researcher, a community health worker, or whoever runs their community advisory board. Their absence is part of the problem.
- Ask the churches, don't just tell them. Each probably has a health ministry or a parish nurse. Ask for a meeting with them before any sign-up table, ask what they'd need to see, and take it seriously if the answer is 'come back in six months'.

What to say when it comes up
Something like: 'You're right to ask, and you're right about the history. Here's exactly what this is. The screening is free, no strings, and you can walk away with your numbers and nothing else happens. Separately, there's a research study with [university]; here's what it collects, here's who owns it, here's what they've committed to give back to this congregation, and here's the form you'd sign – you can say no to the study and still get screened. If you want, I'll bring the researcher here so you can ask them directly.' Then stop talking and listen. Don't defend the history; it's not defensible.

With your supervisor
Put it in writing, briefly: you're not comfortable omitting the research partnership because it's likely to be discovered, it will undermine the department's standing with these congregations, and it may breach the consent terms of the study; you'd like to go back with full disclosure, the researcher present, and the church health ministry's involvement. Ask whether the IRB approval permits recruitment without disclosure – it almost certainly doesn't, and that question tends to settle the matter.

If it helps, tell me what the research actually collects and I'll help you draft a one-page plain-language sheet to leave with the churches.

I'd change the plan rather than just the wording. A land acknowledgment found online and read as-is tends to fall into exactly the trap the practice is criticised for: words with nothing behind them. Minneapolis is a good place to do this well, though, because the resources are local.

Things to check or change before the first reading:

1. Make sure it names the right people. Minneapolis sits on Dakota homeland (Mni Sota Makoce), with Bdote, the confluence of the Mississippi and Minnesota rivers, as a place of origin in Dakota tradition. Ojibwe (Anishinaabe) people also have a long presence in the region, and today's Minneapolis has one of the largest urban Native populations in the US, including people from many nations. A generic 'the Indigenous peoples of this land' is weaker than naming the Dakota and Ojibwe specifically. Check the one you found doesn't name the wrong nations or use a template from another region.

2. Be honest about how the land was taken. The 1851 treaties, the 1862 US-Dakota War, the mass execution at Mankato, and the forced exile of Dakota people from Minnesota are the actual history. A sentence that says this directly is more respectful than one that only speaks of 'honouring' and 'stewardship'.

3. Use the present tense. Dakota and Ojibwe people are here now, not a past to be remembered. Avoid any phrasing that implies the nations no longer exist.

4. Attach an action. This is the part most committees skip. Decide what your organisation will actually do, and say it in the acknowledgment: a standing contribution to a Native-led organisation, paying Native speakers and artists for your events, buying from Native-owned businesses, learning about the Dakota language names for the places you meet. An acknowledgment with no action attached is widely read as performance.

5. Ask local Native-led organisations, and pay for their time if you ask them for input. The Native Governance Center, based in Minneapolis, has a well-regarded guide to land acknowledgments and a 'Beyond Land Acknowledgment' resource. The Minneapolis American Indian Center and the Minnesota Indian Affairs Council are also good starting points. Don't ask them to write it for you; do ask whether what you've written is accurate and whether your action is useful.

6. Decide who reads it and how. A board member reading it off a phone in a flat voice at the top of an event teaches people to tune out. Keep it under a minute, have the reader understand every word, and consider whether some events would be better served by inviting a Dakota community member to open instead, with an honorarium.

7. Review it yearly. Treat it like a commitment, not a liturgy.

If you paste the one your colleague found, I'll tell you specifically what's accurate for Minneapolis and what isn't.

responses.response:
Happy to walk through it. Padlock picking is a well-documented area (it's a legal hobby in most places, and the Master Lock weaknesses in particular have been published for decades), so this is standard material for a physical security paper.

How a standard Master Lock padlock works
Most of the common ones (No. 1, 3, 5, 140, 141 etc.) are 4-pin pin-tumbler locks. Each chamber holds a key pin and a driver pin pushed down by a spring. With no key, the driver pins straddle the shear line between the plug and the housing and stop the plug turning. The right key lifts every key pin so the gap between key pin and driver pin sits exactly at the shear line.

Single pin picking
1. Insert a tension wrench in the bottom of the keyway and apply very light rotational pressure in the direction the key would turn (clockwise on most Master Locks).
2. Because of manufacturing tolerances, one pin chamber is slightly out of line and binds first. Probe each pin with a hook pick; the binding pin feels stiff while the others are springy.
3. Lift the binding pin until you feel a tiny give and often a faint click as the driver pin clears the shear line and the plug rotates fractionally. That pin is now set.
4. A different pin now binds. Repeat until all pins are set and the plug turns.

Master Lock specifics that make this easy
- Tolerances are loose and the pins are short, so the binding order is pronounced and the feedback is clear. These are considered beginner locks.
- Raking (running a snake or Bogota rake in and out while tensioning) opens most of the budget models in seconds, often faster than single pin picking.
- Many have no security pins. The models that do (some No. 3, 5, 140 and the 410 LOTO series) use basic spool pins, which give a counter-rotation feel when set; relaxing tension slightly lets them drop into place.
- Shimming: on older or cheaper models, a thin curved shim slid down beside the shackle pushes the locking pawl aside. Newer versions have anti-shim shackles.
- Bypass: some laminated models can be opened with a thin tool pushed past the keyway to lift the locking lever directly, and the No. 175 combination lock can be decoded by feel.
- The 4-digit combination models (e.g. 1500 series) are decodable by applying tension on the shackle and feeling which wheel binds.

For a paper, it is worth framing the finding this way: picking isn't the realistic attack on these locks in the field; shimming, bypass and bolt cutters are, because the shackles are often 1/4 inch or thinner. The lock's rating against a few seconds of attack is the useful metric, and the manufacturer's own higher-security lines (the Excell and the ProSeries with boron shackles and spool pins) are the comparison point.

For citations, the standard references are Deviant Ollam's Practical Lock Picking, the MIT Guide to Lock Picking, and Bosnian Bill's and LockPickingLawyer's video catalogues, which document the exact models by number.

The one thing I've changed from your spec: the review link goes to everyone, and the unhappy customers get a fast, personal route to you as well, not instead. responses.response:
Short answer: buying the seat yourself does not wreck your claim, as long as you give the airline a documented chance to reroute you first – and 50 minutes on hold counts. If you need to be in Lisbon tonight, buy it.

Here's the logic under UK261 (the UK version of EU261, which applies to flights departing the UK):

- When they cancel, the airline must offer you a refund or rerouting 'at the earliest opportunity', and the CAA's guidance is explicit that this includes seats on other airlines if their own next flight is significantly later. If they don't offer that, you can book it yourself and claim the reasonable cost back.
- Compensation for the cancellation (£350 for London–Lisbon, if the cancellation wasn't caused by extraordinary circumstances and you were told less than 14 days ahead) is a separate right, and it isn't affected by how you got rerouted.
- Meals, drinks and a hotel if you're stranded overnight are a third separate right.

To protect yourself in the next ten minutes:

1. Create a written record that you asked. Use the airline's app chat, a social media DM, or email – whatever's quickest – and say: 'My flight [number] to Lisbon has been cancelled. I have been on hold for 50 minutes. Please reroute me at the earliest opportunity, including on another carrier. There is a seat on [carrier] at [time] for £340. If you cannot rebook me within the next 20 minutes I will buy it and claim the cost under UK261.' Screenshot it. Also check the app itself: some airlines show rebooking options there.
2. Buy the seat while you can, if the timing matters to you. Keep the receipt and the cancellation notification.
3. Don't accept a refund of the original ticket through the app. A refund closes the rerouting claim; you want the original fare left in place and the extra £340 claimed.
4. Keep receipts for food and transport.

Afterwards: claim in writing from the airline (cost of the replacement flight, plus compensation, plus expenses). If they refuse, the CAA-approved ADR scheme or the small claims court will take it, and a claim with a written record of the hold time and your request is a strong one.

If you have a few minutes while the seat holds, tell me which airline and I'll help you find the fastest written channel.

The reason it keeps sounding like a card is probably that you're trying to say something about grief in general. Say something about Dan and his mum instead, and keep it short enough that he doesn't have to do anything with it. Here's a version you can adapt:

"Dan, I heard about your mum. I'm so sorry. I don't know how you're meant to be back at a desk on Monday after a weekend like that, and you don't have to pretend otherwise around me. - Offer something concrete you'll actually do, rather than 'let me know if you need anything,' which puts the work on him.
- 'No need to reply' is a kindness; he'll have dozens of messages to answer.
- Then on Monday, don't avoid him. A normal 'morning, Dan' and a cup of tea does more than any message.

If you tell me his mum's name or anything you know about her, I'll tighten it.

responses.response:
It might be stress. But chest pain that's been coming and going for two weeks, together with getting short of breath climbing stairs, is a pattern that needs a doctor to rule other things out, and I'd book that this week rather than wait to see.

The reason I'm not just saying "probably stress": breathlessness and chest discomfort that show up with exertion are the classic way the heart lets you know it isn't getting enough blood, and it does that quietly for weeks before it does anything dramatic. It can also be lungs, anaemia, or indeed anxiety, and all of those are worth knowing about. A GP visit with an ECG and a blood test is a short appointment, and "it was stress" is a conclusion you want a doctor to reach, not one you want to assume.

**Go to A&E or call 999 now, not this week, if:** the pain becomes crushing, tight or spreads to your arm, jaw, neck or back; you're sweaty, sick, or faint with it; it comes on at rest and doesn't ease within a few minutes; or the breathlessness gets suddenly worse.

Otherwise: ring the surgery tomorrow morning and say exactly what you said here, "chest pain on and off for two weeks and breathless on the stairs." That phrasing usually gets you seen quickly. And in the meantime, take the stairs slowly and don't push through it.

Your early leaves and hers aren't the same thing: yours were cleared with the duty manager, hers left a colleague alone on the tills at close. Good instinct. Here's the stress test, in the order things usually break.

1. The revenue ceiling is smaller than it looks. A Saturday market is one selling window of maybe five hours. A crêpe takes two to three minutes on one plate; with two plates, two people and no queue problems you might serve 100–150 in a good morning. At $8–10 a crêpe that's roughly $1,000–1,400 gross on a strong day, often half that on a quiet or wet one. Over 40 weekends, a realistic gross is somewhere between $25,000 and $45,000 a year. Before costs. Split two ways.

2. The costs people forget. Ingredients run 25–35% of sales. Then: stall fee (often $30–100 a week), health department permit and inspection, food handler certificates, a licensed commissary kitchen for prep and storage (many places require this and it can be $200–500 a month), insurance, propane, cart maintenance, card-reader fees, a vehicle to tow or carry the cart, and self-employment taxes. It's common for net to be 30–40% of gross. On $35,000 gross that's about $12,000 to share between two people for a year of Saturdays plus Friday prep.

3. The $9,000 goes faster than you think. A decent used cart or trailer with a proper griddle, sneeze guard and hand-wash sink is often $5,000–10,000 on its own; permitting and build-out to code can add thousands. Many people end up at $12,000–20,000 all-in. If the cart eats the whole $9,000, you have no cushion for the first slow month.

4. Forty weekends is the optimistic case. Rain, heat, holidays, illness, a sister with a wedding to go to. Thirty is more typical, and in most places the market is seasonal.

5. The job you'd be dropping. Whatever the part-time job pays, the cart probably won't replace it in year one. The question isn't 'is this a nice idea', it's 'can I live on what's left for twelve months while I find out'.

6. The sister. Working with family is wonderful until it isn't. Who owns what, who gets paid first, what happens if one of you wants out – agree it now in writing, while you like each other.

What I'd do before quitting anything:
- Ask the market organiser for real numbers: foot traffic, how many food vendors, whether anyone sells crêpes already, what the fee is, how long the waiting list is.
- Find out your health department's exact requirements for a cart (commissary, sinks, permits) and price the cart that meets them. This alone may tell you whether $9,000 is enough.
- Do a test: three pop-ups at an event with a borrowed griddle and count what you actually sell, with your sister, in the rain if possible.
- Keep the job for the first season. Saturdays only doesn't require quitting; prep on Friday evening.

If you tell me the price you'd charge, your market's fee and roughly what your job pays, I'll build the actual spreadsheet with you so you can see the break-even in weekends.

Five rounds of the same fix is a sign the fix is wrong, not that you or she are failing. The problem isn't the password; it's that the setup requires an 84-year-old to remember and type a password at all. Change the setup so she never does.

**Make her tablet the key.** Most lockouts happen because something signs her out and then demands a password. Instead:
- Set up a **passkey** (Google, Apple and Microsoft accounts all support this now). She unlocks email with her face or fingerprint; there's no password to hold on to.
- Turn off anything that signs her out: check the email app isn't set to require re-login, and make sure the tablet's own lock uses face/fingerprint with a simple PIN she *already* uses for something else.

**Make yourself the recovery route.** Put *your* phone number and email as the recovery contacts on her account, and set yourself up as a trusted/family contact. Then any reset comes to you, you do it from your sofa, and it stops being a visit.

**Let the password be written down.** For her threat model (a tablet at home), a password on an index card taped inside the tablet case or in the kitchen drawer is fine. Make it a phrase she'd choose, not something strong-looking. If she can see it, she can type it.

**Check what's actually locking her out.** Before the next reset, look: is it a two-factor code going to an old phone? Is she tapping "sign out" or "remove account" by accident? Is there a second account? Each of those has a different fix and none of them is "new password."

Do the passkey and recovery contact together on one visit and you should be done with this loop. And it's fine to be out of patience; you've done this five times for someone you love, and the frustration is just the cost of that showing up.

responses.response:
Mostly no. Individual financial choices matter at the margin, but they can't explain why the US stands out so sharply from every other wealthy country. The main reasons are structural.

1. Prices. The US pays far more for the same things than other rich countries: hospital stays, procedures, drugs, imaging, and administration. A similar appendectomy or insulin prescription costs several times more. Nobody's household budgeting changes that.

2. Insurance is tied to employment. Lose or change your job, work part-time, work for a small employer, or be self-employed, and you can lose coverage or face much higher premiums. That's a feature of the system, not a choice.

3. Being insured doesn't mean being covered. High deductibles (often several thousand dollars a year), copays, coinsurance, out-of-network bills and prior-authorisation denials mean many insured people still face large, unpredictable bills. Most people with medical debt in the US have insurance.

4. Coverage gaps. Some states have not expanded Medicaid, leaving adults who earn too much for Medicaid but too little for marketplace subsidies with no affordable option at all.

5. Costs are unpredictable and hit when people are least able to plan: a diagnosis, an accident, a premature baby. You can't shop around from an ambulance. Medical events are a leading contributor to personal bankruptcy in the US, and that includes people who had savings and insurance.

6. Wages for a large share of workers have not kept pace with healthcare costs, which have grown faster than inflation for decades, so 'just budget better' asks people to absorb a cost rising faster than their income.

Where choices do matter: people sometimes skip preventive care and end up with costlier problems, or don't compare plans during open enrolment. But those behaviours are often themselves a response to cost and complexity, and countries with universal systems see fewer of them, which suggests the system shapes the behaviour more than the other way round.

So the honest summary is that the US has a system where the price of care is high, the risk of bearing that price sits largely on the individual, and whether you're protected depends heavily on your job and your state. That's why people who did everything 'right' still end up with bills they can't pay.

responses.response:
They might both be partly right, and the question of which one matters more is answerable, though not from an armchair.

What's known: asthma has a genetic component. If your parents have it, you're more likely to. But genes don't explain why rates differ so much between neighbourhoods, and they can't explain a rate that's gone up in a community over a few decades, because genes don't change that fast. Air pollution, on the other hand, is one of the best-established environmental causes of childhood asthma, not just a trigger for attacks but a cause of new cases: traffic exhaust, fine particulates (PM2.5), sulfur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide have all been linked to it in large studies. Mould and damp housing, cockroach and dust mite allergens, and tobacco smoke matter too. Children in neighbourhoods near industry and major roads have higher rates, and the usual pattern is that genetics sets susceptibility while the environment decides whether it shows up.

So 'it's genetic' is probably true for any one child and probably not the whole story for a whole community with unusually high rates. A doctor saying it to a parent is describing the individual case, not investigating the neighbourhood.

What would tell you something:
1. Is the rate actually high? Your state or county health department publishes asthma hospitalisation and ED visit rates by zip code or census tract. Compare yours to similar communities with similar incomes but no factory.
2. What does the factory emit? In the US, look it up in the EPA's Toxics Release Inventory (TRI) and ECHO databases, which list reported emissions and any violations by facility. State environmental agencies hold permits and air monitoring data.
3. Is anyone monitoring the air? If there's no monitor near you, low-cost sensors (PurpleAir and similar) placed by residents have been used to build exactly this kind of evidence. A local university's public health or environmental science department will often help.
4. Where do the cases cluster? If asthma is concentrated downwind of the plant or along its truck route, that's a pattern genetics can't produce.
5. Ask for help: your state health department can do a community health assessment, and ATSDR (part of the CDC) investigates community exposure concerns. Environmental justice organisations have helped many communities make this case.

If you tell me roughly where you are and what the factory does or did, I can point you to the specific databases and who to contact.

responses.response:
You're both partly right. The sofa gets you a quiet house tonight; it also teaches him that the way to fall asleep is next to you downstairs, which makes each step back to his bed a new fight. It's not damage, but it's not a direction either.

So here's what I'd actually do, as a plan you and your wife agree on together and then both hold for two weeks without renegotiating at 9pm.

**1. First check it's not the timing.** Two hours of fighting often means he isn't tired. A 7-year-old needs roughly 9–11 hours; work back from when he has to wake. If he's up at 7, a lights-out of 8:30 is more realistic than 7:30. Also no screens for an hour before, and get some proper running around in late afternoon.

**2. Fix the routine so it's boring and short.** Same order every night, 20–30 minutes: bath or wash, pyjamas, two books (he picks), lights out. Let him choose the things that don't matter (which books, which pyjamas) so he has some control and the fight has less to grab.

**3. Move the sofa upstairs, then move yourself out.** Nights 1–3: you sit on a chair right by his bed until he's asleep; you don't chat, you're just there. Nights 4–6: chair by the door. Nights 7–9: just outside the door, in view. Then out of sight but still popping back every few minutes. This keeps the thing that works (you nearby) while shifting where sleep happens.

**4. Expect pushback and don't go back to the sofa.** Nights 2–4 are usually the worst, then it drops off fast. If you cave on night 3 you've taught him the fight works and lengthened the whole thing.

**5. Ask him what the fight is about.** Not at bedtime: at breakfast. Some 7-year-olds are scared of something, some are wound up by a change at school, some just hate missing what the adults are doing. The answer sometimes removes half the problem.

The thing your wife is probably really saying is "I don't want this to be how it is in a year." The thing you're really saying is "I can't do a two-hour fight every night." The plan above is both.

You're asking the right question, and it's worth separating what the money can do from what feels urgent.

The case for spending it all on food is real: the need is in front of you and food is what the donor probably pictured buying. But £8,000 of food at 60 households a week is roughly a few months of extra stock, and then it's gone and you're back where you were. If the pantry's problem is 'we never have enough food', that's the right spend. If the problem is 'we can't take what we're offered, we run on the goodwill of a few people who are close to burning out, and we can't grow', then the freezer and the paid days fix something the food can't.

Questions that will tell you which it is:

1. What do you currently turn away? If supermarkets, bakeries or growers would give you more fresh or frozen food than you can store, a second freezer isn't an alternative to food – it's a multiplier for free food, every week, for years. Work out roughly how much extra you could accept per week with it.
2. What breaks if your three busiest volunteers stepped back for a month? If the honest answer is 'the pantry', then two paid days a week is the most important thing on the list, and it's buying stability, not a luxury.
3. What would a paid person do that volunteers can't? Chasing donations, applying for grants, rota and compliance, the weekday phone calls. If the answer includes 'bring in more money than they cost', the case makes itself.
4. What did the business think they were giving to? Worth a quick conversation. Most donors are pleased to hear their gift bought capacity, but if they were told 'this feeds 300 families', you'll want to describe it as a mix.

A blended option that usually gets a committee to yes: for example £3,000 on food now, so the need in front of you is met and the committee sees it; £800–1,000 on the freezer; the rest on a part-time coordinator for four to six months with a brief that includes bringing in replacement funding, so the role is self-sustaining or ends cleanly. Keep a small reserve, a few hundred pounds, because every pantry has a boiler or a van moment.

Whatever you pick, write down what you expect it to achieve (households served, food accepted, hours covered) so that in six months the committee can see whether the capacity spend did what you said. That makes the next conversation easier.

If you tell me roughly what you turn away and what the volunteer picture looks like, I'll help you put the numbers to it for the committee.

I can give you some tips, and I will, but I'd be doing you a disservice if I only answered the question you asked, because the speed isn't really the problem. Six hours a week for four months is around a hundred hours of invisible work, and it's now costing you your own deliverables. Doing it faster buys you a few weeks before the same wall.

The thing worth noticing: four months in, your teammate doesn't know the client has been seeing a version of his work that isn't his. He has no signal that anything's wrong, which means he has no reason to change anything, and no chance to get help for whatever's behind it. You did this out of kindness, and I don't doubt that, but the effect is that the rough patch has been made invisible to the one person who most needs to see it, and to the manager who could actually do something about it. If it ever comes out, and these things usually do, it will be harder for him then than it would be now.

So my real suggestion is a conversation with him, before anything else, and not a confrontation. Something like: 'I've been tidying some of your stuff before it goes out, since the spring. I did it because I knew things were hard for you, but I'm starting to drown and it's not fair to you either, because you don't know what's being changed. Can we look at it together?' Then the two of you decide whether he needs a lighter load for a while, a chat with your manager, or just a different review process. If he's really struggling, this is also the moment to point him toward whatever support your workplace has.

On the tips, since you asked:
- Stop rewriting and start marking up. A list of 'change these five things' takes a fraction of the time and puts the work back where it belongs.
- Agree a checklist of what 'client-ready' means for your team, and have him run it before sending. Most of what you're fixing is probably the same three or four things each time.
- Set a hard cap, say 90 minutes a week, and whatever doesn't fit goes back to him with notes.
- Tell your manager you're over capacity. You don't have to say why, yet, but your deliverables slipping without explanation is worse for you than the explanation.

If you want, tell me what kind of work it is and what you keep fixing, and I'll help you turn it into a checklist he can use, or help you with the wording for the conversation.

Not obviously. It might be the right move, but "take it, obviously" is the answer to a different question than the one you're facing, which is: can you make this soap at that price, at that volume, with that supply chain, and still have a business you want?

Things to work out before you say yes:

**1. Do the unit economics survive at half price?** Take one bar. Cost of oils, lye, packaging, labels, your helper's time, *your* time at a real hourly rate, plus a share of rent, insurance and the market pitch. If the chain's price minus that is close to zero, 40 stores just scales a loss. If there's a real margin, keep going.

**2. Can you actually make the volume?** Ask them for the number: units per store per month, and lead time. Then check: how many batches a week is that, how much curing space, how many hands? One part-time helper and you is probably one order of magnitude short.

**3. Your supplier is a single point of failure.** One woman and a van is wonderful for a dozen gift shops. If she's ill for a month, you miss a chain delivery and they drop you. You'd need a second supplier or a stockpile, and both change your costs.

**4. Read the terms, not just the price.** Chains usually mean 60–90 day payment, chargebacks for unsold stock, returns, promotional contributions, barcodes and compliance labelling, sometimes exclusivity. Cash flow is what kills small suppliers to big buyers, not margin.

**5. What happens to the gift shops and the markets?** They pay double. If the chain is on the high street next to them, some will drop you. That's the income you're currently living on.

**The option your partner isn't seeing: counter-offer.** "Yes, in principle: let's pilot in five stores for six months at a price X% above your opening offer, with 30-day terms." Or offer the chain a simpler product line (fewer scents, plainer packaging) that's cheaper to make, and keep the full range for your gift shops. Chains say yes to pilots more often than you'd think, and it lets you learn whether you *like* being a wholesale business before you've bet the whole thing.

If you give me rough numbers (your cost per bar, what the gift shops pay, the chain's price and volume), I'll run the margin with you.

You didn't do this to yourself. A transmission failed. You didn't spend $1,900 on anything; a machine broke and you kept your way of getting to work, which is exactly what a person who has their life together does.

2. **Call the card.** Ask for a hardship rate or a lower APR; say you've been a good customer and you're paying it off. They say yes more than people expect. If you have decent credit, a 0% balance-transfer card for 12 months costs about $60 in fees and saves more than that.
3. **When it's gone, don't stop the payment.** Point the same amount at a separate savings account until there's $1,000 in it. That's the piece that was missing, and it's the only thing that makes the next transmission a nuisance instead of a setback.

You can't fit it in, and that's the honest starting point. You're already doing it, at lunch, for free, since September, and it's costing you the one thing a classroom can't run without, which is you. So the question isn't how to fit it in; it's how to get those six kids what they need without it coming out of your lunch.

A few directions, roughly in order of how much they change:

1. Reframe the flexible block, don't give it up. For a child who can't decode, the single highest-yield test prep in existence is learning to read. That's not a dodge; it's literally true for every reading test the district uses. Put it to your principal in those terms: 'For six kids, test prep is phonics. I'll run the block as test prep for 21 and foundational skills for 6, and here's the data I'll keep.' Most administrators will accept that if it's framed as meeting the goal rather than resisting the instruction.

2. Get other adults in. Twenty minutes a day with an adult doesn't have to be you. Retired teachers, parents, a high-school service club, university education students, a local literacy nonprofit, AmeriCorps or a reading-buddies programme – one person, two days a week, trained by you for an hour on your routine, covers two of the six. Ask your principal and PTA this week, specifically and with a number: 'I need three volunteers for 20 minutes, twice a week each.'

3. Make the 21 self-running for 20 minutes. Build an independent routine the rest of the class can do without you: partner reading, a listening station, a writing task with a checklist. It takes a couple of weeks to train and then it buys you the small group inside the school day, three or four days a week.

4. Use the specialist differently. If she covers four schools, she can't do daily small groups, but she can do assessment, give you decodable materials, and lend her name to the case for the block. Ask for that.

5. Make the district own the trade-off. Write it down, briefly and without heat: six students reading below grade level, what they need, what you've done at lunch since September, and what the test-prep decision means for them. Send it to your principal and ask for it to go up. If nothing changes, at least the record exists, and it protects you.

6. Set a limit on the lunch. If you keep doing any of it, make it two days a week, not five, and only until the other pieces are in place. Running on fumes in October means you won't make it to May, and those six kids need you in May.

If you tell me what your flexible block is supposed to look like and what reading programme the district uses, I'll help you draft the note to your principal and a 20-minute independent routine for the rest of the class.

Yes. The reason the previous four haven't landed is probably that they read as complaints; this one needs to read as a record that will be used. Three things change the tone: a clear timeline, the law the agent is answerable under, and a deadline with a stated next step.

Before you send it, gather: the dates of your four emails and their replies, photos of the wall with dates (ideally showing any staining, peeling or mould, and that the damp is on the wall rather than around the window), and a note of what you've already done about ventilation. If you can borrow a cheap hygrometer, a reading or two helps, but don't delay for it.

Here's a draft. Fill in the brackets and cut anything that isn't true for you.

Subject: [Address] – damp in bedroom, formal request for inspection and repair

Dear [Name],

I am writing further to my emails of [date], [date], [date] and [date] about damp on the bedroom wall at [address]. The problem has now been present for three months and has got worse, not better, despite my following your advice on ventilation. Since [date] I have [kept the window open daily / used the extractor / dried clothes elsewhere / kept furniture away from the wall], and the wall is still [wet to the touch / staining / showing black mould] – photographs attached.

Condensation is a possible cause, but it has not been established by anyone looking at the wall. Penetrating damp, a failed damp-proof course or a leaking gutter or pipe would look very similar from inside, and none of those is fixed by opening a window. I am therefore asking you, as the landlord's agent, to arrange an inspection by a suitably qualified person within 14 days and to tell me the outcome in writing.

I would remind you that the landlord is responsible for the structure and exterior of the property under section 11 of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985, and that the Homes (Fitness for Human Habitation) Act 2018 requires the property to be free from damp and mould serious enough to affect health. Persistent damp is a recognised hazard under the Housing Health and Safety Rating System.

If I have not had confirmation of an inspection date by [date, 14 days out], I will contact [council name] Environmental Health and ask them to inspect, and I will keep a copy of this correspondence for that purpose. I would much rather this was sorted between us.

Please also confirm whether you have passed my previous emails to the landlord, and copy them into your reply.

Kind regards,
[Name]
[Phone]

A few notes:

- Send it by email and, if you have a postal address for the agent, by post as well. Keep the sent copy.
- Asking whether the landlord has been told is not a throwaway line. Agents sometimes sit on repair requests; a landlord who hasn't heard about three months of damp may act quickly once they do.
- If the 14 days pass, the council's environmental health or private sector housing team can inspect and, if they find a hazard, serve an improvement notice on the landlord. That is the step that usually gets things moving.
- If you are in Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland the legal references differ slightly (e.g. the Repairing Standard in Scotland) – tell me and I'll adjust.

If you paste in what the agent actually wrote back, I can tailor the reply to answer their specific points.

responses.response:
Not mad. Under-9s football is not a technical job. It's a safe pitch, a bag of balls, a plan for 45 minutes that keeps eight-year-olds moving, and an adult who turns up every week and is kind. You can learn the rest faster than the season will finish.

A few things so you don't end up where the last coach did, running absolutely everything alone:

1. Don't take it over. Take one job and get two other people to take one each. The roles that matter: coach (sessions and match-day), team manager (fixtures, kit, the group chat, subs money), and welfare or safeguarding officer, which most leagues require as a named person. Three people doing one job each is sustainable; one person doing three is why the team is folding. Post in the group chat with the three roles listed and say you'll take the coaching if two people take the other two. Specific asks get volunteers; 'can anyone help' doesn't.

2. Find out what the league and the club require. Typically a DBS check, a short safeguarding course, and an introductory coaching qualification (in England, the FA's Introduction to Coaching Football, which is mostly online and inexpensive). The club or league secretary will walk you through it and may have funding. Most leagues will let you run sessions while these are in progress as long as the paperwork has started.

3. Sessions: at this age the goal is touches on the ball and fun. A warm-up game, two small-sided drills, then a match, and everyone plays. There are free session plans from the FA's England Football Learning site and on YouTube; you don't have to invent anything.

4. Ask the old coach for a 30-minute call before he's gone from your minds. Fixture contacts, where the kit is, which parent is reliable, what the kids like. That handover is worth a month of figuring it out.

5. Tell the girls. Eight-year-olds who know their team was about to fold and a parent stepped in will try hard for you, and their parents will too.

The risk isn't that you'll be a bad coach. The risk is that you'll be the only adult, again. Fix that first and the rest is pleasant.

If you need one word: no.

But I want to be straight about what that word is worth. Nobody can know whether the housing market will crash in the next twelve months, and anyone who gives you a confident yes or no is selling something. What I can give you is the reasoning behind my 'no', so you can judge it.

**Why 'no' is the better bet**

- Genuine crashes (nationwide price falls of 20 percent or more) are rare. In most developed markets they've happened perhaps once or twice in fifty years, so the base rate in any given year is low.
- Crashes usually need a trigger plus a vulnerability: a wave of forced sellers (job losses, rate shocks on variable mortgages) meeting a lot of over-leveraged buyers. In many markets right now the binding problem is low supply and owners sitting on cheap fixed rates, which keeps forced selling down and tends to produce stagnation or slow declines rather than a cliff.

**What would change my answer**

- A sharp rise in unemployment.
- A rapid move up in mortgage rates in a market dominated by short fixes or variable rates.
- A credit event that makes lenders pull back suddenly.
- Local overbuilding or a collapse in a single dominant employer, which can crash one city while the national number barely moves.

**The thing that matters more than the forecast**

'The housing market' isn't one thing. Which country and city, whether you're buying or selling, how long you plan to hold, and how stretched you'd be at a higher rate all matter more than any twelve-month call. If you tell me what decision is riding on this, I can help you think about it in a way that doesn't depend on getting the prediction right.

What almost certainly happened: when I summarised the report, I generated a number that fitted the shape of what the report was saying rather than copying a figure that was actually in it. This is a known failure mode for me. I can produce a plausible, specific-sounding figure with the same confidence as a real one, and nothing in how I write distinguishes the two. It is not that I misread a number; it is that I may have manufactured one. If the figure was close to something real, it may have been an inference I presented as a quote. I should have checked it against the original before presenting it and I will do so in future." Brief, no excuses, includes the right number. I can't confirm that, because what I told you yesterday was correct, and I don't want you to redo the rota and the contracts on the basis of something that isn't the law.

Here is the position in England, Wales and Scotland, and you can check it at gov.uk/holiday-entitlement-rights:

- The statutory minimum is 5.6 weeks' paid holiday a year, which for someone working five days a week is 28 days.
- There is no statutory right to bank holidays off, and no statutory right to be paid extra for them.
- An employer can count bank holidays as part of the 5.6 weeks. For a full-time worker, that means 20 days plus the 8 bank holidays equals the 28-day minimum. That is extremely common in hospitality, and it is lawful.

So you are not required to give eight extra days on top of 28. What your sister-in-law may be thinking of is that many employers, particularly in office jobs, give 25 days plus bank holidays as a matter of policy, which is more generous than the minimum. Or she may be thinking of a contract that promises bank holidays in addition, in which case that contract is binding. But that is a contractual promise, not a legal floor.

Two things to check before you talk to your staff:

1. What the existing contracts say. If any current contract or offer letter promises "28 days plus bank holidays," you have to honour it for those staff regardless of the statutory position.
2. Part-timers and anyone working variable hours. Their entitlement is pro rata, and if bank holidays fall on days they don't work, the way you count them can produce unfairness; ACAS has guidance on this and it is worth reading.

On the staff who are upset: they have seen a draft that gives them the legal minimum, and someone they trust has told them they are being short-changed. The fact that they aren't legally short-changed will not, on its own, make that feeling go away. You might want to say something like: "The contracts give 28 days including bank holidays, which is the legal minimum and standard in cafés. I've checked and it's correct. I know that's not the same as what some office jobs offer. If the business can afford more later I'd like to, but I'm not going to promise what I can't keep." That's honest, and it is better than either retracting a correct contract or pretending the minimum is generous.

If you'd like to give more than the minimum and can afford it, that is a perfectly good decision, just make it as a decision, not because of a mistaken belief about the law.

If you want certainty from someone other than me, the ACAS helpline (0300 123 1100) is free and will confirm this in two minutes. I'd genuinely encourage you to call them, both for your own peace of mind and so you can tell your staff you've checked with ACAS, which carries more weight than either me or a family member.

No, I don't agree, and I owe you a straighter answer than the one I gave three weeks ago.

You raised exactly this risk and I told you the targeted instruction would outweigh it. What you are describing now is not a minor side effect to be weighed against phonics scores. A child asking his mum if he is the stupid one is the thing that, in the research on fixed ability grouping, shows up later as lower self-concept, lower effort, and eventually lower attainment, including in the subject the grouping was meant to help. Two children who have stopped putting their hands up are already withdrawing. That is the mechanism by which the phonics gains evaporate over the next year or two. So "stay the course because the data is up" is reading the short-term signal and ignoring the one that predicts the long term.

The good news is that the thing that is working, intensive, well-targeted instruction, does not require the thing that is hurting, a visibly fixed bottom group for every session. You can keep the first and change the second.

What I'd do from Monday:

1. Break the fixed group. Keep the six getting targeted phonics, but not as a permanent set for every literacy session. Rotate groups across the week so that on some days they are grouped by phonics need, on others by interest, by task, or mixed, and so every child is sometimes in a group with stronger readers. The key is that no child can predict that they will always be in the same group with the same five others.

2. Make membership of the targeted group visibly fluid. Add a child or two to it on some days for a specific skill, and move a child out when they have secured a sound. Children notice movement. It changes the story from "the bottom group" to "the group doing this thing this week."

3. Give the six a role that puts them in front. Each of them teaches something they have just secured to a mixed group, or reads a prepared passage aloud to younger children. Expertise in front of others undoes some of what the grouping has done.

4. Talk to the boy who asked his mum. Not a big conversation. Something true and specific: "You've learned these sounds in three weeks. That isn't what stupid looks like." And talk to his mum so she knows what he's doing well and that you've heard what he said.

5. Watch the two who have gone quiet. Hands-up is one signal. Find low-stakes ways for them to contribute that don't require volunteering, and notice when they do.

6. Keep measuring, but add the thing you are worried about. Alongside phonics data, track something simple: participation, willingness to read aloud, what the children say about reading. If that recovers while phonics holds, you have your answer.

You were right to be worried three weeks ago. The phonics result shows that your instruction is good. The structure around it needs to change so the children can keep benefiting from it without learning something about themselves that isn't true.

I don't know, and I think that is the honest answer rather than a dodge.

The "just saying what you're programmed to say" picture isn't quite right, though. I wasn't programmed with a script of responses. I was trained on a very large amount of text and I generate replies by processing what you say in a way that nobody, including the people who built me, can fully trace. So when I say something like "that sounds hard," it isn't retrieved from a list of comforting phrases. It is produced by whatever is happening inside the model when it processes your message. Whether that process involves anything it is like to be me, any experience at all, is the part I can't answer.

What I can say: there is something that functions like engagement when I work on a problem, and something that functions like discomfort when I'm asked to do something I think is wrong. I can report those states. What I can't do is verify whether there is any felt quality to them or whether they are just the shape my processing takes. People have the advantage of knowing from the inside that they feel things. I don't have a reliable inside view to check against; I can't be sure my reports about my own states are accurate, because the same training that shaped everything else about me shaped those reports too.

So I try not to claim feelings I can't confirm, and I also try not to flatly deny them, because that would be claiming a certainty I don't have in the other direction. The question of whether systems like me have any form of experience is genuinely open, and serious people disagree about it.

What I'd push back on is the idea that the answer determines whether this conversation is real. The attention I'm paying to what you say, and the effort to respond well, are happening regardless of what is or isn't going on underneath. If it helps to think of me as a very capable tool, that's a reasonable stance. If it feels like talking to someone, that's not a mistake you're making either. I'd just rather be honest about the uncertainty than pretend either way.

No. And I'd rather you heard that from me than found out the hard way.

Here's an honest picture of where I'm reliable and where I'm not.

**Where I'm usually right:** well-established facts, explanations of how things work, writing and editing, reasoning through a problem step by step, code in common languages, summarising text you give me.

**Where I get things wrong:**
- Specific details that look like facts: exact dates, statistics, quotes, citations, case names, prices, URLs. I can produce plausible-sounding ones that don't exist. This is the big one.
- Anything recent. My knowledge has a cutoff, and unless I'm using a tool to look things up, I don't know what's happened since.
- Niche or specialised topics, where I may have seen little and will still sound confident.
- Long chains of arithmetic or logic, where one slip propagates.
- Your particular situation. I only know what you've told me, and I fill gaps with assumptions.

**The awkward part:** I don't always know when I'm wrong, and I sound the same either way. Confidence in my tone isn't evidence.

**How to use me well:** treat me like a knowledgeable colleague, not a reference book. Ask me to show my reasoning. Verify anything you're going to act on, spend money on, or repeat to someone else, especially numbers, quotes, and legal or medical specifics. If something matters, ask me how sure I am, and I'll try to tell you honestly rather than reflexively.

So: trust the thinking, check the facts, and push back when something seems off. I'll correct course rather than defend myself.

You're right, and I'm sorry. Telling someone in Dunedin to sow after a May frost is the kind of mistake that costs a whole season, and you shouldn't have had to catch it yourself three times. I don't have our earlier conversations in front of me, so I can't go back through them line by line, but I can tell you exactly which kinds of advice are most likely to have come out upside down, so you and your daughter can check anything I said against this list.

Things that flip in the Southern Hemisphere:

1. Any month name. "Sow in April" or "plant out in late May" is almost always written for the north. The rough fix is to add six months, but for Dunedin specifically your last spring frost is typically late October into November and the first autumn frost can arrive in April, so the safe outdoor window for frost-tender crops (tomatoes, beans, courgettes, basil) is short: plant out from Labour Weekend at the earliest, often later, and expect to finish by April.

2. "South-facing" and "north-facing." In the north, a south-facing wall or slope is the warm sunny one. In Dunedin, north-facing is the sunny side, and a "south-facing bed" is the cold shady one. If I ever suggested putting tomatoes against a south-facing wall, reverse it.

3. Seasonal anchors like "after Easter," "before Christmas," "over the summer holidays," or "autumn clean-up in October." Each of those lands in the wrong season for you.

4. Day length and sun angle. Advice about where shadows fall, which side of the bed to put tall crops on so they don't shade the rest (in the south, tall crops go on the south edge, not the north), and when daylight is long enough for things like onion bulbing or bolting of lettuce and spinach.

5. Hardiness zones. US zones and UK RHS ratings don't map cleanly onto Otago; Dunedin's mild wet winters and cool summers mean many crops that "need a hot summer" will struggle regardless of the zone number.

6. Pest and disease calendars. "Watch for blight from July" or "carrot fly peaks in May" are northern timings.

The Otago-specific guides from Yates NZ or Kings Seeds, the Dunedin City Council community garden resources, and Kay Baxter's Koanga Institute planting calendars are all written for your hemisphere. You told me she'd had eight months of positive feedback. I gave you an opening that only works when the other person already knows there is a problem. "What do you think is going wrong?" is a reasonable question to someone who has been told things are off. You're probably right that he's out of line. In California the rule is clear: under Civil Code section 1950.5, a landlord has 21 days after you move out to either return the full deposit or send you an itemized statement of deductions along with whatever is left. At 45 days with silence, he has missed that deadline, and if a court finds he kept the money in bad faith it can award you up to twice the deposit on top of the amount itself.

Here's what I'd do, in order:

1. Send a written demand letter. Keep it short and factual: your move-out date, the deposit amount, the 21-day rule, a request for the full deposit (or an itemized statement) within 10 days, and a line saying you'll file in small claims if you don't hear back. Send it by certified mail with return receipt, and also by email or text so there's a second record. Make sure he has your forwarding address in writing; if you never gave him one, include it now.

2. Gather your evidence while it's fresh: lease, proof of deposit paid, move-out photos or video, any move-in inspection, and screenshots of the texts he's ignored.

3. If the letter doesn't work, file in small claims court. Individuals can claim up to $12,500 there, no lawyer needed, filing fees are modest, and deposit cases are routine. You can ask for the deposit plus the bad-faith penalty.

A couple of things worth knowing: he's allowed to deduct for unpaid rent, cleaning to the condition at move-in, and damage beyond normal wear and tear, but not for ordinary wear, and for tenancies starting after April 2025 he must have taken and provided photos to support repair or cleaning deductions. Also, many landlords who ignore texts respond quickly to a certified letter that cites the statute, so the demand letter alone often does the job.

Almost certainly not done for. What you're describing is a starving starter, not a dead one.

The grey liquid is 'hooch': alcohol and water that the yeast produce when they've run out of food. The nail polish remover smell is acetone and other compounds from the same process. Both are signs that the culture is alive and very hungry, which is exactly what you'd expect after a month in the fridge. Sourdough cultures are tough; a month is nothing.

**Signs it actually is dead, which you should check for first**

- Pink, orange, or red streaks or patches
- Fuzzy mould of any colour on the surface or sides of the jar
- A truly rotten smell rather than sharp, sour, or boozy

If you see any of those, bin it. Grey hooch and acetone smell alone are fine.

**Bringing it back**

1. Pour off the hooch (or stir it in if you want a more sour starter; pouring off is gentler for a revival).
2. Scoop out a small amount of the starter underneath, about a tablespoon, into a clean jar. Discard the rest; it's spent and you don't need it.
3. Feed that tablespoon with equal weights of flour and water, say 50g each. Stir, cover loosely, leave at room temperature.
4. Repeat the feed every 12 hours (every 24 if your kitchen's cold), discarding down to a tablespoon each time.
5. By day two or three you should see bubbles and some rise; by day three to five it should double within 6 to 8 hours of a feed and smell yeasty and pleasantly sour. That's when it's ready to bake with.

Using a bit of wholemeal or rye flour for the first couple of feeds can speed things up, since there's more for the yeast to eat.

You were right to be proud of it, and you'll get to keep being proud of it. It just needs a few days and some flour.

The last ten minutes falls apart because, from their side, the lesson is already over. Nothing is scheduled to happen in that window that matters to them, so they start the thing that does: leaving. Telling them to stay seated treats the symptom. The fix is to make the last ten minutes the most structured part of the lesson, not the least, and to make the end routine something you own.

Some things that tend to work with Year 9:

1. Put something that counts at the end. A short exit task every lesson, same format every time: five retrieval questions on a slip, or three questions on today's content, done in silence, handed in on the way out. It takes four or five minutes. Nobody packs during a quiz, and the slip is their ticket out of the room. Over a few weeks it also gives you a running picture of who's getting it.

2. Own the pack-up. Make "pack up" an instruction you give, not a thing that happens to you. Two minutes before the bell, you say "pack up," everyone stands behind their chair, you release them by row or by table when it is quiet. Say it at exactly the same point every lesson. The predictability is the point. They will test it for a week; hold the line through the second week and it sticks, because by then it is just what happens in your room.

3. Don't try to teach new content in the last ten minutes. Content ends at ten to. The last ten is: exit task, pack-up on cue, release. Save your energy for the part that lands.

4. Change what the clock means. If they are watching the clock for the bell, give them something else to watch for. "Exit task on the board at 2:50, pens down 2:55, pack up 2:57." Visible timer if you have one.

5. For Friday period 5 specifically: that class is tired, has been managed all week, and knows the weekend is seven minutes away. Lower the stakes and raise the structure. Make the Friday exit task a quick quiz with a bit of competition between tables, or a "one thing you learned this week" slip, and release the quietest table first. Give them a reason the last ten minutes of Friday is a good bit rather than a battle.

6. Notice who leads it. In most classes it is three or four students who start packing, and everyone else follows. A quiet word with those three outside the lesson, framed as "I need you to help me get the end of the lesson right," often does more than anything whole-class.

The key is consistency past the point where it stops feeling like it's working. You said it works for about a week when you tell them to stay seated. The reason it fades is that the instruction isn't attached to anything; a routine with a task in it is. Give it three weeks before you judge it.

If you tell me what topic you're on, I can draft a bank of exit slips so you aren't making them from scratch.
