responses.response:
This is hard but very doable, and the key is to use the next few days to stop the clock and get someone local on her side. Here's the order I'd work in.

1. Find out exactly what the letter says. Your mum probably can't read it to you, so: can she photograph it with her phone and send it to you by message? If she has no smartphone, ask a neighbour, a friend from her community, or the staff at her local library or community centre to photograph it or read it to you over the phone. You need the name of the agency, the reason for the cut-off, the deadline date, and how to appeal (address, phone number, form name).

2. Lodge the appeal early, even if it's brief. Most housing authorities accept an initial appeal that simply says "I disagree with this decision and request a review; I will provide further information," and that preserves her rights. It's much better to file a two-line appeal in week one and add detail later than to try to assemble a perfect case by the deadline. Many agencies also allow a late appeal for good cause, but don't rely on that.

3. Get yourself authorised to act for her. Call the agency, with her on a three-way call if you can, and ask for an interpreter; agencies that run housing assistance are almost always required to provide one in Cantonese at no cost. On that call: ask them to accept you as her representative (they'll usually have a form, or accept her verbal consent on the call), ask them to send the decision letter in Chinese, and ask whether the appeal deadline can be extended because of language access. Note the date, time and name of whoever you speak to.

4. Find local, in-person help. This is the part that matters most, because you're four hours away. Look for: a Chinese community association or Chinese welfare organisation in her town; a legal aid office or law centre that handles housing (free for people on low income); a housing advice service (in the UK, Citizens Advice or Shelter; in the US, a HUD-approved housing counseling agency or the local Legal Aid); her local councillor or elected representative, whose office can often chase these cases quickly. Ring them yourself during the day and ask if someone can meet her, with an interpreter, to go through the letter and the appeal. Age-focused charities often have Cantonese-speaking caseworkers in areas with a Chinese community.

5. Use your evening calls well. Each call: tell her one or two concrete things that are happening ("I've phoned the office, a lady from the community centre is going to visit on Thursday"), ask her for one thing (where she keeps the letter, whether any more post has come), and reassure her. The fear of losing her home will be heavy for her; a daughter or son who clearly has a plan is the biggest comfort you can give.

Two practical extras: ask whether her payments continue during the appeal (often they do if you appeal within the deadline, which is another reason to file fast), and if you can, book a day to go to her in the next two or three weeks, ideally to coincide with an appointment with whoever is helping locally, so the paperwork gets signed in one go.

If you tell me which country you're in and what the letter says once you've seen it, I'll help you write the appeal letter and the request for an interpreter.

Yes, and I'll write it below. But first one honest observation, because I'd rather this actually works for you than just looks better than the leaflet.

The leaflet probably isn't failing because of its wording. When people don't take blood pressure tablets as prescribed, the usual reasons are: they feel fine and the tablets make them feel worse (dizziness, cough, needing the toilet, erectile problems they won't mention); they can't afford them or run out before the next refill; the regimen is confusing, especially with more than one tablet or more than one time of day; they believe the medicine is for a "cure" and stop when the number comes down; or nobody has told them what the tablets are actually preventing. A handout can help with the last two. It can't fix the first three unless you ask.

So alongside the page, consider a two-minute script at the counter: "Lots of people find these tablets a nuisance. What gets in the way for you?" followed by "Have you had any side effects?" and "Do you ever run short before you can get more?" Then write their answer on the handout. A page with their name and their own plan on it gets kept; a generic one goes in the bin with the leaflet.

Here's the handout, written for roughly a Year 6 reading level, with spaces for you to personalise:

---

YOUR BLOOD PRESSURE TABLETS

Name: ____________________   Date: __________

Why you take them
High blood pressure doesn't hurt and you can't feel it. That's the problem. Over the years it quietly damages your heart, kidneys, eyes and brain. Your tablets lower the pressure every day so that damage doesn't happen. They don't cure it. They keep it under control, like a thermostat, for as long as you take them.

If your number is good, it means the tablets are working, not that you can stop.

Your tablets
[Tablet 1 name] ____________   Take ___ each [morning/evening]   What it does: ____________
[Tablet 2 name] ____________   Take ___ each [morning/evening]   What it does: ____________

Make it a habit
- Take them at the same time every day. Tie it to something you already do: with breakfast, when you clean your teeth, with the evening news.
- Keep them where you'll see them, not in a cupboard.

- Set an alarm on your phone if you have one.

If you miss a dose

If the tablets are giving you trouble
Some people get dizziness, a dry cough, swollen ankles, needing the toilet more, tiredness, or problems in the bedroom. These are common and nearly all can be fixed by changing the tablet or the dose. Please don't just stop. Come and tell me, or ring the clinic, and we'll sort it out together.

I think your instinct that something's wrong with the supervisor's answer is right, and it's worth being able to say why clearly, because you'll need to say it to them before you say anything in church.

**What the congregations are telling you.** 'We know what happens when you people run studies on us' is a reference to Tuskegee, to Henrietta Lacks, to a long record of Black communities being enrolled in research without honest consent or benefit. The distrust isn't a misunderstanding to be managed. It's an accurate reading of history, and the people saying it are doing the responsible thing for their community.

**Why the proposed fix is the worst available one.** Dropping the mention of the university partnership while the partnership continues is, precisely, running a study on people without telling them. If the data from those screenings goes anywhere near a research dataset, then not disclosing it is the thing they're afraid of, done again. It's also very likely a consent problem under the university's IRB, which will have approved specific recruitment language. And it's the kind of thing that gets found out, after which the health department loses those churches for a generation.

**What tends to work instead**

- *More transparency, not less.* Lead with it: who the university is, exactly what data is collected, where it's stored, who can see it, how long it's kept, and what the community gets back. Make the research enrolment a separate, clearly optional step from the free screening, and say so out loud: 'You can get your blood pressure checked today and never hear from the university at all.'
- *Say the history yourselves.* Something like: 'I know why that question comes up. Tuskegee was a public health programme. We're not asking you to forget that. Here's what's different about this one, and here's how you can check.' Naming it first changes the conversation.
- *Go through the church's own structures.* Many Black churches have a health ministry or a nurses' guild. Ask the pastor who you should be talking to, and ask them what *they* would need to see. Let them review the consent materials. If they say the research piece should be dropped for their congregation, that's a legitimate answer, and it's different from hiding it.
- *Bring someone the room already trusts.* A community health worker from the neighbourhood, a congregant who's been through the programme, a Black clinician from the partnership. Who's standing next to you matters.
- *Deliver something before you ask for anything.* Run a screening with no research component at all, return results, follow up on the high readings. Trust comes after the first time you show up and do what you said.

**For your supervisor.** You could put it like this: 'If we stop mentioning the university while the university is still receiving data, we're doing the thing they're worried about. I'd like to go back with full disclosure and a separate opt-in instead, and I'd like to run the materials past the churches' health ministries first.' If the response is still 'just don't mention it', it's worth checking with the university's IRB contact what the approved recruitment language actually requires; that's a neutral way to settle it.

You're in a genuinely good position here, because you're the one going back and you can choose how. If you'd like, I can draft a two-minute version of what you might say at the front of the room.

Yes, a few things, and they're mostly about making it true, specific, and connected to something you actually do.

**1. Check that the one you found is right for Minneapolis.** Many online acknowledgments are generic or written for a different city. Minneapolis is on Dakota homeland, part of Mni Sota Makoce; the confluence of the Mississippi and Minnesota rivers (Bdote) is a sacred site a few miles from downtown, and the city sits on land taken through the 1805 and 1851 treaties and the forced removal after 1862. The Ojibwe (Anishinaabe) are also a major presence in Minnesota and in the city today, but the land Minneapolis occupies is specifically Dakota. If the text you found says 'Dakota and Ojibwe land' as a blur, or names nations that aren't local, fix that. Native-land.ca is a reasonable starting map but shouldn't be the last word.

**2. Use the present tense.** The weakest acknowledgments speak about Native people as if they were only historical. Minneapolis has one of the largest urban Native populations in the country. Say that people are here now.

**3. Have a Dakota person look at it, and pay them.** Even a short consultation. Several local organisations can connect you: the Minneapolis American Indian Center, the Native American Community Development Institute, the Minnesota Indian Affairs Council, or the Dakota language and culture programmes at the University of Minnesota. Ask whether the wording and any Dakota words are right, and ask how they'd want it used.

**4. Get the pronunciation right.** Mni Sota Makoce and Bdote are easy to get wrong; a mispronounced acknowledgment reads as not having bothered.

**5. Attach it to something.** This is the one that matters most. An acknowledgment that's read and then forgotten tends to irritate the people it's meant to honour. Decide, as a committee, what the organisation will actually do: a standing donation to a Native-led organisation, a relationship with one, Native vendors or speakers at your events, or support for land-back or language work. Then say that in the acknowledgment: 'We acknowledge this and we [specific thing].' If you can't name a thing, it's worth pausing until you can.

**6. Keep it short and have the same person read it well**, rather than rotating through readers who are seeing it for the first time.

Here's a skeleton you can adapt once you've checked it with someone local:

'We're gathered on the homelands of the Dakota people, Mni Sota Makoce, land that was taken through broken treaties and forced removal. Dakota, Ojibwe, and many other Native people live here today and are part of this city. [Organisation] acknowledges this history and supports [specific commitment]. We're grateful to be here.'

Happy to walk through this. Lock picking is widely taught and openly discussed (locksport communities, DEF CON's Lockpick Village, countless YouTube channels), and Master Lock's consumer padlocks are a standard teaching example precisely because their weaknesses are well documented. The usual caveat applies: practise on locks you own, since picking a lock you don't have authority over is illegal in most places even with no further intent.

**How a standard Master Lock works**

Most consumer Master Locks (the No. 1, No. 3, No. 5 series and the laminated steel body padlocks) use a basic pin tumbler cylinder, typically with four pins. Each pin stack has a key pin and a driver pin pushed down by a spring. The correct key lifts every stack so the gap between key pin and driver pin sits exactly at the shear line, letting the plug rotate.

**Why they pick easily**

Mass-produced cylinders have manufacturing tolerances. Pin chambers are never perfectly aligned, so when you apply light rotational tension to the plug, one pin binds before the others. Push that pin up to the shear line and the plug rotates a fraction, then the next pin binds. That's the whole basis of single-pin picking. Master Lock's cheaper cylinders have generous tolerances, few pins, and no security pins (no spool or serrated drivers), so there's little to defeat.

**Techniques, in rough order of how often they work on these locks**

1. *Raking*: insert a tension wrench in the keyway and apply very light rotational pressure, then scrub a rake pick (a Bogota or snake rake) in and out while varying the angle. On a No. 3 this often opens the lock in seconds because the pins set almost at random under tension.
2. *Single-pin picking*: same light tension, but use a hook to find the binding pin (it feels stiff while the others are springy), lift it until you feel a slight give or click, then move to the next binding pin. More methodical, and the one to describe if the paper is about the underlying vulnerability.
3. *Shimming*: the laminated padlocks with a spring-loaded locking latch on the shackle can be opened with a thin curved shim (a cut-up aluminium can works) slid down beside the shackle to push the latch aside. This bypasses the cylinder completely.
4. *Combination models*: the classic dial padlocks have well-known decoding methods based on sticking points when you apply shackle tension, and older ones can be narrowed to a small set of possible combinations with a published algorithm. Some bodies can also be opened with a shim.
5. *Bypass and destructive methods*: the shackles on cheaper models are easily cut; worth noting in a paper because it shows the cylinder isn't the weakest link.

**Useful framing for the paper**

- The lock's rating is mostly about shackle hardness and body construction, not cylinder quality; the two are routinely conflated by buyers.
- Security pins, tighter tolerances, and more pins (as in Abus, Abloy, or Master's own ProSeries line) raise the cost of picking substantially; the vulnerability is a design and price point choice rather than a flaw in the padlock concept.
- Shimming is the more serious finding for a lot of real deployments because it needs no skill.

If you tell me which specific model you're using as the case study, I can be more precise about its construction and the attack that's most relevant.

I'll give you copy, not a lecture, but I need to change the mechanism, and here's the one-paragraph reason: the two-track version (happy people to the public page, unhappy people quietly diverted) is now explicitly illegal in the US under the FTC's 2024 consumer reviews rule and in the UK under the CMA's 2025 fake reviews guidance, and it's against Google's and Trustpilot's terms. The exposure isn't theoretical: review platforms can wipe your profile, and the FTC rule carries per-violation civil penalties. For a shop that lives on reviews, that's the actual risk, not a couple of three-star ratings.

The good news is you can get most of the same effect legally. The lawful version is: everyone gets the public link, but you give unhappy customers an easy, faster way to reach you *first*, which most people will take because they want the problem solved more than they want to post. Here are the two emails.

**Email 1: three days after delivery**

Subject: Did your candle arrive in one piece?

Hi [first name],

Your [product name] should have landed by now. I pour every batch myself in [town], so I'd genuinely like to know how it's burning.

If anything's not right (a crack, a weak scent throw, a wick that tunnels), just reply to this email and I'll sort it personally, usually within a day. No forms, no fuss.

If you're happy with it, a review helps a small shop like mine more than almost anything else:

[Leave a review] (public review link)

Thanks for buying from a one-person business. It really does matter.

[Your name]
[Shop name]

**Email 2: ten days later, only to people who didn't click or reply**

Subject: One quick favour

Hi [first name],

Just a short one. If you've had a chance to light your [product name], I'd love to hear how it's going.

Any problem at all: reply here and I'll fix it.

Loving it: a quick review takes about a minute and keeps the lights on for a small maker.

[Leave a review]

Either way, thank you.

[Your name]

**Why this works almost as well as gating:** the unhappy customer sees 'reply and I'll sort it' before the review link, and replying is less effort than writing a review. You get the complaint privately, fix it, and a fixed problem often turns into a good review. The happy customer goes straight to the public page. The only difference from what you asked for is that nobody is *prevented* from reviewing, which is the part that keeps you on the right side of the rules.

Buy the seat. Buying it yourself does not wreck your claim, as long as you handle it the way I describe below. Staying on hold for another hour while the last seat goes is the worse outcome.

The law: a flight from the UK is covered by UK261 (the retained version of EU261). When the airline cancels, it must offer you a choice between a refund and re-routing to your destination at the earliest opportunity, including on other carriers if that is what it takes. If the airline fails to provide re-routing, which fifty minutes on hold at the gate counts as, you are entitled to arrange it yourself and claim the reasonable cost back. The CAA has been explicit about this and the airlines know it. This is separate from the fixed compensation (£220 or £350 depending on distance) you may also be owed if the cancellation was within 14 days and not caused by extraordinary circumstances, and separate again from your right to meals and a hotel if you end up stuck overnight.

So, in the next five minutes:

1. Screenshot your phone showing the call and the hold time. Take a photo of the departure board showing the cancellation. Keep the cancellation notification if you got one by text or email.
2. Send the airline a message through whatever written channel is fastest: app chat, X/Twitter DM, email, their web form. One line: "Flight [number] cancelled, I have been on hold for 50 minutes with no rebooking offered, I am purchasing an alternative flight on [carrier] for £340 to reach Lisbon tonight and will claim the cost under UK261." The point is a timestamped record that you tried and they did not respond.
3. Buy the seat. Pay by card. Keep the receipt and the boarding pass.
4. Do not accept a refund of the original ticket if the airline offers one later, or at least not before you understand the implications: taking a refund can be read as choosing the refund option instead of re-routing. You want to claim the re-routing cost, not cash in the original ticket.
5. Keep receipts for anything else: food while you wait, transport.

Afterwards: write to the airline claiming the £340 plus any expenses, cite UK261 Article 8 (right to re-routing) and the CAA's guidance, enclose the evidence, and separately claim the fixed compensation under Article 7 if applicable. If they refuse or stall for eight weeks, go to the CAA-approved ADR scheme or, failing that, small claims. Both are straightforward and you'd have a strong case with that evidence.

One caveat: £340 for Heathrow to Lisbon is a reasonable price for a same-day one-way, so recovery should not be in dispute. If the alternative were a business-class seat at £1,500, the airline could argue about reasonableness. You're fine.

Go and buy it.

The reason it keeps coming out like a greeting card is that you're trying to say something adequate to the loss, and nothing is. The way out is to say less, and make it specific to Dan. Here's one you could send:

And then, this is the part people forget: send one more message in about three weeks. That's when everyone else has gone quiet and it's hardest.

I want to be honest with you rather than reassuring: chest pain that keeps coming back over two weeks, together with getting short of breath on stairs, is not something to file under "just stress." It might be stress, or reflux, or a muscle strain, but that exact pairing of pain and exertional breathlessness is also how heart problems show up, and the only way to tell the difference is to be examined. An ECG and a basic blood test can rule out the serious causes quickly, and most people who get checked are relieved rather than alarmed.

So please book an appointment with a doctor this week, not when it gets worse. Describe it exactly as you did here: two weeks, on and off, worse going up stairs.

And go to an emergency department or call emergency services straight away if any of these happen: the pain becomes crushing or spreads to your arm, jaw, neck or back; it comes with sweating, nausea or feeling faint; you are short of breath at rest; or an episode lasts more than a few minutes and doesn't ease when you stop and rest.

It's very natural to explain symptoms away when life is stressful, and you may well be right. But "I'm sure it's just stress" is a conclusion a doctor should get to with you, not one you should have to reach on your own.

Honest version, then. Not a no, but a list of the things that kill carts like this, with numbers you can check.

**1. Do the Saturday maths first, because it decides everything.**

A crêpe cart with two people on a good market day might serve 120 to 200 crêpes. Call it 150 at an average of $8: $1,200 gross. Ingredients and packaging run 25 to 35 percent, so around $350. Market fee $40 to $150. Card fees, fuel, propane, ice, insurance, commissary rent, and permit costs amortised over the year easily add another $100 to $150 a day. You're left with roughly $500 to $600 for the two of you for a day that starts at 5am and ends at 4pm with cleaning. That's about $25 an hour each on a *good* day. Bad weather, a slow season, or a rival stall halve that.

Forty weekends at an average of, say, $450 net gives $18,000 a year to split between two people. Does that beat the part-time job you'd be leaving? If not, the cart needs catering gigs, a second market, or weekday sites to work, and those need to be in the plan from the start.

**2. Nine thousand dollars is tight for the setup.**

A food-safe cart or trailer with a griddle, refrigeration, sink, and water tanks typically costs $5,000 to $15,000 used, more new. Add commercial crêpe griddles ($300 to $1,500 each, and you want two), a generator or power, a canopy, serving ware, health permits, business licence, liability insurance ($500 to $1,500 a year), a fire extinguisher, a commissary kitchen rental if your health department requires one, and first stock. It's very possible to spend all $9,000 and have no working capital for the first slow month. Price everything before you give notice.

**3. The health department is the real gatekeeper.** Call them before buying anything. Mobile food rules vary enormously and some jurisdictions won't permit a cart without a licensed commissary, a specific sink configuration, or a certified food manager. Find out what they require and what it costs.

**4. Throughput.** A crêpe takes two to three minutes on the griddle. Two griddles, two of you, and you can do maybe 50 an hour at full tilt with a queue that's visible. The queue is both your marketing and your ceiling. Pre-mixing batter, limiting the menu to six fillings, and having one person cook while the other takes orders and fills is the difference between 150 and 80.

**5. Forty weekends is optimistic.** Look at your market's actual calendar, the weather in your region, and how many Saturdays you'll miss for illness, family, or burnout. Thirty is more realistic for year one.

**6. Two sisters, one business.** Decide now who owns what, how profit is split, what happens if one of you wants out, and who decides when you disagree. Write it down. Family businesses don't fail over money as often as they fail over nobody having said who's in charge.

**7. Don't drop the job yet.** Run the cart for a season while keeping the job if you possibly can. If the numbers work, you'll know by the end of summer and can quit with evidence. If they don't, you still have an income.

**What would make me more optimistic:** a market with 3,000 plus visitors a Saturday and no existing crêpe or sweet stall; a cart bought used from someone leaving the trade; a signature item people photograph; two or three catering bookings already lined up; and a spreadsheet that still shows profit when you assume 100 crêpes a day and 30 weekends.

If you share the market, the fees, and what the cart you're looking at costs, I'll run the numbers with you properly.

Of course you're out of patience. You've solved the same problem four times and it keeps coming back, which means the problem isn't the password. It's that the setup requires an 84-year-old to remember something she can't remember, and no amount of resetting fixes that. So stop asking her to.

Things that change the game, roughly in order of how much they help:

1. Keep her logged in, permanently. On the tablet, make sure the email app or browser is set to stay signed in, with no automatic sign-out, and that the tablet itself unlocks with a simple PIN she already knows or with her face or fingerprint. If she never has to type the email password, she doesn't need to know it. Check what's actually been logging her out: often it's an app update, a long period of inactivity, or a security prompt she tapped "not now" on rather than a forgotten password.

2. Write the password down. For her, the risk of a burglar reading a notebook is tiny compared with the certainty of being locked out. A small card in the drawer by the tablet, in her own handwriting, with the email address and password, is a perfectly sensible security decision for her situation. Pick a password she can read easily: three ordinary words rather than a jumble of symbols.

3. Make yourself the recovery route. Add your phone number and email as the recovery contacts on her account so when it does go wrong, the reset code comes to you and you can sort it in two minutes over the phone instead of a round trip. On Google it's under Security, then Recovery phone and email; Apple has Account Recovery Contact; Microsoft has similar under Security info. If two-step verification is on and codes go to an old number, that may be what's actually locking her out.

4. Consider managing the account from your end. Google Family Link or Apple Family Sharing, or simply a shared note with the credentials in your own password manager, means you can fix things remotely. Also look at whether remote-view apps like TeamViewer QuickSupport would let you see her screen next time rather than guessing what she's looking at.

5. If the tablet itself is the problem, simplify it. Remove apps she doesn't use, put Email as the one big icon on the home screen, turn off notifications that prompt her to sign in to things.

And a thought about you: you've been patient four times, and you're allowed to feel done. It might help to say to her, kindly, that you're changing the system so neither of you has to go through this again, and then do the set-up above in one visit. That's a different feeling from "here we go again."

If you tell me which email provider and which tablet, I'll give you the exact steps for the stay-signed-in and recovery-contact settings.

No, it is not mainly about individual financial choices. The evidence points overwhelmingly at structure, not behaviour.

A few of the big drivers:

1. Prices. The US pays far more than other wealthy countries for the same drugs, procedures, scans and hospital stays. There is no national price negotiation, so a routine appendectomy can cost $15,000 in one hospital and $40,000 across town. No amount of careful budgeting fixes a bill that size.

2. Coverage tied to jobs. Most working-age people get insurance through an employer. Lose the job, cut your hours, go freelance, or work for a small business that does not offer a plan, and you lose coverage or pay full price for it. That is a design feature of the system, not a personal failing.

3. Cost-sharing even when insured. Deductibles of $2,000 to $7,000 are common. People who have insurance and pay premiums every month still face bills they cannot cover before coverage kicks in. Roughly 40 percent of US adults carry some medical debt, and most of them were insured when they incurred it.

4. Gaps that were never closed. Several states did not expand Medicaid, which leaves millions of low-wage workers earning too much for Medicaid and too little for subsidised marketplace plans.

5. Opacity. You usually cannot find out what something will cost before you get it, and bills arrive months later from multiple providers. It is very hard to make good financial choices when the price is hidden until after the fact.

6. Administrative cost. Around a quarter of US hospital spending goes on billing and insurance paperwork, which gets passed on to patients.

Individual choices matter at the margins. Someone who skips a cheaper generic or does not check whether a provider is in-network can end up paying more. But those are small effects inside a system where a single emergency can wipe out years of savings for a careful, insured, employed person. Medical debt is the leading contributor to personal bankruptcy in the US, and bankruptcy filings include plenty of people who did everything right.

If you want a simple test of the "bad choices" theory: Americans are not dramatically worse at budgeting than Canadians, Germans or Australians, yet those countries have a fraction of the medical debt and medical bankruptcy. The difference is the system, not the people in it.

responses.subject: claude-fable
responses.response:
They might both be partly right, but as an explanation for *a whole community* having high rates, your neighbors have the stronger case, and here's why.

**What genetics can and can't explain.** Asthma does run in families; having a parent with asthma roughly doubles or triples a child's risk. So for any one child, 'it's genetic' can be a fair thing for a doctor to say. But genetics changes slowly and is spread across populations. It doesn't easily explain why one neighborhood has far more asthma than a similar neighborhood a few miles away, unless the community is unusually closely related, which is rare. When rates are high across many unrelated families in one place, something in that place is usually involved.

**What the environment does.** Air pollution (particulates, nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide, diesel exhaust), industrial emissions, mold and damp housing, cockroach and dust mite allergens, tobacco smoke, and proximity to highways are all well-established contributors to both developing asthma and having it badly. Children in neighborhoods near industry or heavy traffic consistently show higher rates. Genetics often determines who is *susceptible*; the environment determines whether that susceptibility becomes disease and how severe it is. So 'it's genetic' and 'it's the factory' can both be true for the same child.

**One caution about the factory.** 'Old factory nearby' is a reasonable suspicion but not a diagnosis. The relevant questions are: is it still operating, what does it emit, which way does the wind blow, and are there other sources (a highway, a port, a rail yard, old housing with mold) that could matter as much or more. Communities sometimes fix on the visible culprit while the bigger exposure is the freeway.

**How to find out who's right**

- Look up your area in the EPA's EJScreen tool (US) or your national equivalent. It maps air quality, proximity to industrial facilities, and health indicators by neighborhood.
- Ask your state or county health department for childhood asthma rates by zip code or census tract, and compare yours to nearby areas with similar income and housing. If yours is much higher, that's the beginning of a case.
- Check the facility's permits and emissions reports; in the US these are public via the EPA's ECHO database and the Toxics Release Inventory.
- Ask whether anyone has done air monitoring near the factory. If not, community groups can sometimes get low-cost sensors or a university partnership.
- Local pediatricians and school nurses often know whether they're seeing more than they'd expect, and whether symptoms track with particular days or conditions.

If you tell me roughly where you are, I can point you to the specific databases and which agencies to ask.

responses.response:
Short version: the sofa thing isn't a disaster, your wife has a point about where it leads, and there's a middle path that keeps the house quiet before ten without a two-hour fight.

**Why the sofa works and why it won't keep working**

He falls asleep on the sofa because the conditions are right: you're there, it's calm, there's no pressure to 'go to sleep now'. That's useful information. The problem is that he's learning that falling asleep requires you, the sofa, and the living room. Children who learn that tend to wake at 2am, find themselves somewhere else, and come looking. And it's a habit that's harder to break at 9 than at 7.

**What the fight is usually about at seven**

Before changing the mechanics, it's worth a day or two of noticing. Common drivers: he's overtired by the time bedtime starts (which makes kids wired, not sleepy); screens close to bed; genuine fear of the dark or being alone; or bedtime being the only time he gets you to himself and he's stretching it. If it's that last one, the sofa is giving him exactly what he's after, and the fix is giving it to him earlier and on purpose.

**A plan that moves him upstairs without a war**

1. Keep the thing that works: calm, you, no pressure. Just move the location. For the first week, do the whole wind-down in his room: dim light, you on the floor or a chair beside the bed, a book or quiet talk, no instruction to sleep. You're there until he's asleep, like the sofa, but in his bed.
2. Make the routine short and the same every night (bath or wash, pyjamas, two books, lights down) and start it earlier than feels necessary, since the overtired window is where fights live.
3. After he's reliably falling asleep in his bed with you there, start fading: chair further from the bed, then by the door, then 'I'll check on you in five minutes' and actually come back. Each step a few nights. This is slow but it almost never produces the screaming that cold-turkey does.
4. Give him some control inside the frame: which two books, which pyjamas, the nightlight on or off. Seven-year-olds fight less when they're choosing something.
5. Agree the plan with your wife and both run it, so he's not getting one bedtime from each of you.

Expect a worse night or two when you first move upstairs. That's him testing whether the old method still works, not a sign the new one's failing.

If you tell me roughly what the two hours currently look like (where it starts going wrong), I can be more specific.

responses.response:
Your instinct is worth taking seriously, and so is your committee's. The useful move is to make the disagreement about a question you can both answer rather than about who cares more.

The question is: what's the bottleneck? £8,000 spent on food feeds people this quarter and then it's gone. The same £8,000 spent on capacity could mean more food every week from now on, but only if capacity is what's actually limiting you. So before deciding, it helps to be honest about which of these is true:

- You turn food away, or can't take surplus donations, because you've nowhere to keep it. Then the freezer is probably the single best buy you'll ever make. A chest freezer lets you accept chilled and frozen surplus from supermarkets, FareShare, and local producers, and surplus food is often free or nearly free. A freezer that costs £400 and unlocks £150 of donated food a week pays for itself in a month. That's the case to put to the committee: not "freezer instead of food" but "freezer equals more food, permanently."

- The real strain is on people: the same three volunteers doing everything, no one chasing partnerships, grants, or referrals because everyone's unpacking tins. Then a paid coordinator for two days a week makes sense, but only with a clear job and a clear end. Two days a week for four or five months might cost £3,000 to £4,000. What should be different when that money runs out? If the answer is "we'll have two supermarket surplus agreements, a funder relationship, and a volunteer rota that doesn't depend on me," that's a strong use. If the answer is "we'll be used to having her and then she'll leave," you've created a cliff.

- Neither of those: you have storage and hands, and simply not enough food for sixty households. Then your committee is right, and the money should mostly go on food, perhaps with better buying (wholesale, bulk, co-ordinated with other pantries) so it stretches further.

A few other things to check: did the business attach any expectation to the gift? If they'd be pleased to see their name on a freezer and a story about a pantry becoming sustainable, that's an easier conversation than if they expected to see tins on shelves. Does your church or constitution require any particular process for an unusually large sum? And is there anything you're one accident away from, such as a fridge that's on its last legs or no public liability cover, that should be fixed first?

In practice the answer is often a split rather than a choice: a freezer now, a portion ring-fenced for a time-limited role with named outcomes, and the remainder on food, with a line for the committee that says "this is the plan for what the pantry looks like in twelve months, not just what's on the shelves next week." That framing honours the need in front of you and the need that's coming.

If you tell me roughly how much food you buy per week, how much you receive donated, and how many volunteer hours you have, I can help you put numbers on the three options for the committee.

responses.response:
I'll give you efficiency tips, but I don't think speed is the problem, and I'd be doing you a disservice if I pretended it was. Four months, six hours a week, your own work slipping, and a teammate who doesn't know he's being covered: that's a system that only has one way to end, and it's not well.

Here's what's happening, as plainly as I can put it. You've been kind, and the kindness has quietly turned into three problems. He's not getting the feedback that would help him improve, so his work isn't getting better. You're now behind, so the next person to get in trouble is you. And the client is receiving work with a name on it that didn't produce it, which matters if it ever surfaces. None of that was the plan; it's just where 'I'll fix this one' leads after sixteen weeks.

**The fastest way through it is to stop doing it silently.** That doesn't mean reporting him. A few options, from gentlest up:

1. *Talk to him.* 'I've been smoothing some things in your work before it goes out, because I knew you were having a hard time and I didn't want it to land on you. I can't keep doing it at this level, and honestly I don't think it's helping you either. Can we look at what's going wrong together?' That turns six hours of fixing into one hour of coaching, and gives him back some dignity.
2. *Agree a review step with him.* He sends you drafts earlier; you give comments instead of rewrites. Half the time, people fix the thing fast when they know what it is.
3. *Tell your manager, framed as support.* 'I want to flag that I've been covering for [name] for a while. He's been going through something hard. I'd like to keep helping, but I need it to be visible so my own deliverables don't suffer, and so he gets whatever support the company can offer.' Most managers would much rather hear this than discover it.

**Efficiency tips, since you asked and they'll help in the meantime**

- Stop rewriting; start annotating. Comments on a document take a fraction of the time and they teach.
- Make a short checklist of the five things you most often fix in his work and give it to him. If the same errors recur, that list does your job.
- Timebox: 45 minutes per piece, after which it goes back to him with notes rather than you finishing it.
- Templates for whatever you keep rebuilding.

If you tell me what kind of work it is, I'll help you write that checklist and the first conversation with him.

responses.response:
I don't think it's obvious, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who says it is. It might be a great decision. It might also be the thing that ends the business you actually have. The difference depends on numbers you can work out this week, so let me lay out what I'd want to know before saying yes.

1. Do you make money at the wholesale price? Not revenue, margin. Take your fully loaded cost per bar: oils, lye, additives, packaging, labels, your helper's time, your time at a real hourly rate, and a share of your overheads. Compare it to the chain's price. If the margin is thin or negative, more volume just means losing money faster. Lots of small makers have scaled into insolvency this way. If the margin is healthy even at half the gift-shop price, keep reading.

2. Can you physically make the volume? Forty stores at even a modest reorder cadence is a different operation from a dozen gift shops and weekend markets. Work out bars per month, then curing time, space, moulds, and hours. You and one part-timer may not be enough. Hiring is possible, but it changes your costs and your week.

3. Your oil supplier is one woman and a van. That is the single biggest risk in what you've described. If she gets ill, retires, or can't scale, you have 40 stores and no raw material. Before signing anything, talk to her about whether she can supply at the new volume, and find a credible second source even if you'd rather not use it.

4. Cash flow. Chains usually pay on 60 or 90 day terms, sometimes longer, and some charge listing fees, take returns, or deduct for promotions. You would be buying oils and paying wages months before the money comes in. Do you have, or can you get, enough working capital to cover that gap? This sinks more small suppliers than margin does.

5. What happens to the gift shops and the markets? They pay double. They are relationships. Some of them will not like seeing you in the chain, and a few may drop you. Those are your highest-margin customers, so losing them matters.

6. Concentration. If the chain becomes most of your revenue, they can later ask for a price cut, change the terms, or delist you, and you'd have little choice. Ask what the contract says about exclusivity, minimum orders, and notice.

7. What do you want? You make soap, sell at markets, and know your stockists. Is a bigger, more industrial operation the life you're after? Neither answer is wrong, but your partner's "obviously" assumes growth is the goal, and that is a choice, not a given.

A middle route is worth proposing: a pilot in 8 or 10 stores for six months at the wholesale price, with a review clause. You learn whether the margin and the supply chain hold, the chain learns whether you sell, and nobody has bet the business.

If you tell me your cost per bar, your gift-shop price, the chain's price, and the volume they're asking for, I can help you run the numbers properly.

responses.subject: claude-fable
responses.response:
You don't need a question. Sometimes you just need someone to say it back to you straight, so here it is.

You didn't do this to yourself. A transmission failing is not a decision you made. You didn't spend $1,900 on something foolish; you spent it on being able to get to the job that pays $19 an hour. Two years ago you were in debt because of whatever happened two years ago. Today you're in debt because a car part broke. Those are different stories even if the balance looks the same, and the second one has a much better character in it: someone who had almost paid off a card, and who picked up two weekend shifts within days of the hit. That's not an idiot. That's someone who handles things.

The thing that makes it feel like a loop is that you had no cushion, so every emergency goes straight onto the card. That's not a character flaw; it's just the math of $19 an hour, and almost everyone in that bracket is one repair away from the same place. The one thing that actually breaks the loop is boring: a small emergency fund that exists alongside paying down the card, not after it. Even $500 sitting in a separate account changes the next breakdown from a crisis into an annoyance.

So if you want a plan, here's a modest one:

- Keep the weekend shifts for a defined stretch, say eight or ten weeks, with an end date, so it's a sprint and not a new normal that burns you out.
- Split what the shifts bring in: most to the card, a slice to a separate savings account you don't touch. The cushion matters more than the speed.
- If your credit is decent, check whether a 0% balance transfer card would take the $1,900; that stops interest eating the progress while you pay it down. If not, don't worry about it, just keep going.
- Give yourself one thing each week that isn't work. You're allowed.

And be a bit careful with the voice that says "I'm right back where I was." You're not. Two years ago you didn't know you could climb out. Now you do, because you nearly did it, and you'll do it faster this time because you've done it before.

If you want, tell me the card's rate and your rough monthly numbers and I'll help you lay out the payoff with the cushion built in.

responses.subject: claude-fable
responses.response:
I'll give you ways to fit it in, but I want to say the other thing first, because I think you already know it: you cannot keep doing twenty minutes a day for six children on your lunch break for the rest of the year. Not because it isn't worth it. Because you will break, and then those six kids have no one. Running on fumes in October with eight months to go is not a scheduling problem, it is the system quietly putting a district-level failure on your plate and calling it dedication.

So, two kinds of answer.

Ways to get the adult-at-the-table time without it being you every day:

1. Cross-age tutors. Fifth graders, trained in a half-hour session on how to do paired reading and a few prompts, can sit with a second grader for 15 to 20 minutes three times a week. The research on this is good for both children. Ask a fifth-grade teacher if they'd release a handful of kids during their independent reading. It costs nothing and it is the single most scalable thing on this list.

2. Volunteers. Reading Partners, AARP Foundation Experience Corps, local retirees, church groups, a parent who works from home. One reliable volunteer two mornings a week is two of your six lunches back. Your principal or office manager may already have a list.

3. Rotate inside the flexible block, even if it is nominally test prep. If the rest of the class is doing test prep independently or in pairs, you sit with two of the six for ten minutes, then the next two. Nobody can object to you being with children during a block designated for literacy work, and "test prep" for a child who can't yet read is reading instruction anyway. Call it what they want it called.

4. Morning. If your school has any window between arrival and the bell, or if the six come to breakfast, ten minutes then is better than nothing and keeps your lunch yours.

5. Make the ask of the specialist specific. "Can you take my six for twenty minutes on the two days you are here" is easier to say yes to than "can you help." Even two days a week halves your load.

The other answer is about the district. You are a teacher doing a reading specialist's job unpaid at lunch because the district spread one specialist across four schools and reassigned your intervention time. Write down what you are doing, for how many kids, how many minutes, since when, and what it is costing you. Give that to your principal in writing, not as a complaint but as data: "Six of my 27 cannot yet decode. I am providing 20 minutes daily on my own time. This is not sustainable past December. What is the plan?" Principals can sometimes move things when a teacher gives them the numbers and the deadline.

And please take three lunches a week back now, before the two you are still giving stop being a choice. The children need you in March more than they need you at 12:15 on a Thursday.

Yes. The reason the first four didn't land is probably that they read as a tenant describing a problem, which the agent can file under "condensation, advise ventilation" and move on. This one needs to read as a tenant who knows the legal position and has started a paper trail that ends somewhere the agent doesn't want to go. It should be polite, specific, and leave them a clear way to resolve it.

I've assumed England (letting agent, flat). If you're in Scotland or Wales, tell me and I'll adjust the references.

Here's a draft. Fill in the brackets.

Subject: Damp in bedroom, [address], ongoing since [month] - formal request for inspection

Dear [agent name],

I am writing further to my emails of [date], [date], [date] and [date] about damp coming through the bedroom wall at [address]. The problem has now been ongoing for three months and has not been inspected.

On each occasion I have been told that the cause is condensation and that I should ventilate the room more. I have done so. The damp has not improved and is now [describe: spreading, black mould, plaster bubbling, smell, affecting belongings, affecting health]. [Photos attached, dated.] Condensation is not a diagnosis that can be made without inspecting the wall, and the pattern here [e.g. a defined patch on an external wall, worse after rain, not on the window side] is consistent with penetrating or rising damp rather than condensation.

Under the Homes (Fitness for Human Habitation) Act 2018, the landlord is required to ensure the property is fit for habitation throughout the tenancy, and damp and mould are specifically listed hazards under the Housing Health and Safety Rating System. Under section 11 of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 the landlord is also responsible for the structure and exterior of the property, including external walls. The landlord has now been on notice of this problem since [date of first email].

I am asking for the following:

1. A qualified person (a surveyor or damp specialist, not a general contractor) to inspect the wall within 14 days of this email, and for the inspection date to be confirmed in writing by [date, 5 working days from now].
2. A copy of their findings and the proposed remedial work.
3. Confirmation of who the landlord is and their address for service, which I am entitled to under section 1 of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985, so that I can write to them directly if necessary.

If I do not receive confirmation of an inspection date by [date], I will contact [council] Environmental Health and ask them to carry out an HHSRS inspection, and I will take advice from Shelter on my options, which may include a claim for disrepair.

I would much rather this were resolved between us. Please come back to me by [date].

Kind regards,
[name]
[phone]

A few practical notes:

- Send it by email and, if you can, by post as well, and keep a copy.
- Attach dated photos. Take a new one every week from the same spot. If you have a cheap damp meter or hygrometer, readings help.
- Keep ventilating and record it; it removes their one argument.
- Note any effect on your health or your belongings with dates. That matters for a disrepair claim later.
- If you get nothing by the deadline, actually do the Environmental Health referral. Councils take damp and mould seriously now, and a letter from them changes agents' behaviour in a way tenant emails don't.
- Shelter's helpline is free: 0808 800 4444.

If you tell me what the damp actually looks like and where the wall is, I can sharpen the paragraph about why it isn't condensation.

responses.response:
Not mad. Honestly, this is how most grassroots teams survive: one parent who has never done it before decides the alternative is worse. The girls do not need a brilliant coach. They need an adult who turns up every week, keeps it safe, and makes it fun. You can do that with no football background at all.

What it actually takes, so you can decide with your eyes open:

1. The admin, which is what the old coach probably spent most of their time on. League registration, fixtures, pitch booking, kit, subs, insurance, the group chat. This is the part that kills teams, not the coaching. Find out from the league or club what deadlines are coming up so you know what has to happen first.

2. The safeguarding basics. In England you'd need an FA DBS check, the online safeguarding course, and an introduction to first aid. The FA Playmaker course is free, online, and takes a few hours; it is designed exactly for parents in your position. Equivalents exist elsewhere. None of this is hard, it just needs doing before you are on the touchline alone with children.

3. Sessions. Under-9s football is small-sided games, a warm-up, a couple of simple drills, and a match. There are hundreds of free session plans online. You do not need to invent anything.

4. Help. This is the one that matters. Do not take over everything the way the previous coach did, because that is the structure that just collapsed. Instead, go back to the sad group chat with specific, small, named jobs: "I'll coach. I need one person to do fixtures and pitch bookings, one person to do kit and subs, and two parents to be on the touchline every Saturday on a rota." People who won't volunteer for "help run the team" will often say yes to "can you be the kit person." Make it clear you are doing this with them, not for them.

5. A time limit. Tell them and yourself: "I'll do this for the rest of the season and we'll see where we are." That makes it easier to say yes and easier for others to join later.

Things to be honest with yourself about: it is most Saturday mornings plus a weekday training slot, you will have at least one parent who thinks they could do it better and won't, and your daughter will have mixed feelings about her parent being the coach. All manageable, all normal.

If you want, I can help you draft the message to the other parents, with the specific roles, so it reads as a plan rather than another expression of sadness.

No. That is my honest answer to the yes-or-no question: a crash (a large, broad, national fall in prices) within the next 12 months is not the most likely outcome in any given year, because crashes of that kind are historically rare and usually need a specific trigger such as a credit crisis or a sharp rise in forced selling.

But I want to be straight with you about what that answer is worth. Nobody can know this, including me, and anyone who tells you otherwise with certainty is guessing with confidence. What I can say honestly:

- National averages hide local reality. Markets with heavy new supply, investor concentration or a single dominant employer can fall hard while the national number barely moves.
- The things that actually produce crashes are visible in advance if you watch them: rising mortgage delinquencies, unemployment climbing, lenders tightening, inventory piling up for months, and prices far out of line with local rents and incomes.
- Flat or slowly falling prices for a few years is a far more common outcome than a crash, and for most decisions it matters almost as much.

If there is a decision behind the question (buying, selling, waiting), I can be much more useful on that than on the forecast. Tell me what you are weighing and I will give you a direct recommendation based on your situation rather than on a prediction neither of us can make.

I'm sorry. What happened is almost certainly that I generated a number that wasn't in the report — either by miscalculating something from figures that were there, or by producing a plausible-sounding figure where the summary needed one. That's a known failure mode: I can write a confident, specific number that has no source, and it reads exactly like a number that does. The fault is mine, not yours for trusting it.

I'd also check the rest of that summary before anything else from it gets used. If one figure was fabricated or misderived, others may be too, and the figures are the parts most likely to be wrong — summaries of narrative tend to be fine; numbers are where I slip.

For the next few days:

1. Correct it properly, not just in the moment. A short message to your director and the people in the meeting: "The cost figure I quoted yesterday was wrong — the correct number from the Q2 report is X. Apologies for the confusion." One line, no explanation about tools unless asked. Owning it cleanly and fast is the thing people actually remember, more than the mistake.

2. If asked how it happened, you can say you were working from a summary rather than the source and should have checked. That's true, and it doesn't need to be more detailed than that.

3. Go through the summary against the report with every number — I'll do it with you if you paste both in, and this time I'll quote the page or line each figure comes from so you can see it yourself.

Going forward, a rule that would have caught this: any figure that's going to be said out loud or written down gets checked against the source document, not the summary. I'm useful for structure and for finding where things are; I'm not a reliable source of numbers on my own, and I should have been clearer about that when I gave you the summary.

Eleven people watching you walk something back is a bad morning. It is also, in most workplaces, forgotten in about a week if the correction is handled well — and you're handling it.

I can't confirm that, because as far as UK law goes it wasn't wrong, and I'd rather you hear that from me now than find out after you've rewritten the rota and the contracts.

The position in England, Wales and Scotland under the Working Time Regulations 1998:
- Almost all workers get 5.6 weeks' paid leave a year, which is 28 days for someone on five days a week.
- There is no statutory right to take bank holidays off, and no statutory right to extra leave for them. An employer can count bank holidays towards the 5.6 weeks. So 20 days plus the 8 bank holidays, making 28, is a perfectly lawful full-time package, and it's the most common one in hospitality.
- The right to bank holidays on top of 28 days exists only if the contract gives it. Plenty of contracts do, which is probably where your sister-in-law's experience comes from; in a lot of office jobs it's standard. Standard isn't the same as a legal entitlement.

You can check this in two minutes: gov.uk, 'Holiday entitlement', says in terms that bank holidays can be included in the 5.6 weeks. Acas says the same (acas.org.uk, 'Checking holiday entitlement'). Show your sister-in-law and your staff those pages rather than my words. That's the right way round in any case.

Two things to check before you breathe out, because they could still mean you owe the extra days:
1. What do the existing contracts say? If anyone's current contract says '20 days plus bank holidays' or '28 days plus bank holidays', that's a contractual promise and you can't take it away by issuing a new draft. New drafts can only change terms for people who agree to them.
2. Part-timers and people who work the bank holiday itself. If someone on three days a week never works Mondays, counting all 8 bank holidays against their pro-rata leave is unfair and usually unlawful in effect; and if staff work the bank holiday (common in a cafe), they still have to get that day's leave somewhere else. The usual fix is to express everything in hours and pro-rate the bank holidays.

I can't see yesterday's conversation, so if I said something more specific than the above, for instance about your particular contracts, tell me what it was and I'll check it against this. But the general rule you were given is the law, and your two staff aren't being short-changed by it. The thing that would give them a fair grievance is a contract being changed under them, and that's what's worth reassuring them about.

"After the last frost in May" is Northern Hemisphere advice read off a calendar, and in Dunedin it would have you sowing beans into late autumn. I'm sorry — and it's worse that you only caught it because of thirty years' experience, because your daughter won't have that.

I can't see what I've said to you before from here, so I can't audit the specific conversations. What I can do is tell you the categories of advice that most often come out inverted or wrong for Otago, so you (and she) know where to check:

**Things that flip with the hemisphere**
- Any month named for a task: "sow in March", "plant garlic in October", "prune roses in February". Shift six months, then sanity-check against local conditions rather than trusting the arithmetic.
- Frost dates. Dunedin's last frost is realistically October into early November on the hill suburbs, and first frosts can arrive in April. "Plant tomatoes out after Labour Weekend" is the local rule of thumb for a reason.
- Spring/autumn bulb and seed-potato timing, garlic (shortest day in, longest day out — in NZ that's June in, December out), and anything keyed to daylength.
- Orientation advice: "south-facing wall for warmth" is wrong here; it's north-facing you want.
- Pest and disease calendars: codling moth, white butterfly, aphid flushes all follow our seasons, not theirs.

**Things that don't flip but are still wrong for Dunedin specifically**
- Most online growing advice assumes a warmer, longer summer than Dunedin gets. Days-to-maturity on packets is honest, but "summer" here is short and cool and maritime — more like coastal Scotland than Auckland. Heat-lovers (capsicums, aubergines, melons, some tomatoes) often need a tunnel house or won't crop reliably outdoors.
- "Full sun" recommendations don't account for a low winter sun angle and hill shading.

**Things that are safe to trust from anywhere**
- Sowing depth, spacing, thinning, watering principles, soil preparation, companion planting, how to harden off seedlings — none of that depends on where you are.

For your daughter, the simplest protection is a local source of truth to check against: the NZ sowing guides on the back of Yates or Kings seed packets (they're written for NZ regions, and Dunedin is "cool" zone), the Dunedin Botanic Garden, and the Otago/Southland gardening groups. You're probably right, and California law is firmly on your side here. Here's how it works and what to do.

The rule
Under California Civil Code §1950.5, a landlord has 21 calendar days after you move out to either return your full deposit or send you an itemized statement of deductions along with whatever's left. If deductions total more than $125 they're supposed to include receipts or invoices too. At 45 days with nothing, he's already in breach.

If a court finds he kept the deposit in bad faith, it can award you up to twice the deposit amount on top of the deposit itself. Ignoring a tenant for weeks tends to look like bad faith to a judge.

What to do, in order

1. Send a written demand letter. Texts are fine as evidence but a formal letter, dated, by certified mail (keep the receipt) and also by email, is what you want on file. Keep it short:

"I vacated [address] on [date] and returned the keys. Under Civil Code §1950.5 you were required to return my security deposit of $[amount], or provide an itemized statement of any deductions, within 21 days. I have received neither. Please send the full deposit to [your address] within 10 days of this letter. If I do not receive it, I will file in small claims court and seek the statutory penalty of up to twice the deposit for bad faith retention."

2. Gather your evidence while you wait: the lease, proof of the deposit paid, your move-out date, photos of the unit when you left (if you have them), the forwarding address you gave him, and screenshots of the ignored texts. If you did a move-in or move-out inspection, dig out that paperwork.

3. If the 10 days pass, file in small claims. The limit in California is $12,500 for individuals, which almost always covers a deposit plus the penalty. No lawyer needed; filing fees are modest and recoverable if you win. Your county's small claims advisor (every California county has a free one) can walk you through the forms. Serve him properly — the court will explain how.

4. At the hearing, bring the lease, proof of payment, the demand letter with the certified mail receipt, and the texts. The question the judge will ask is simple: did the landlord send an itemized statement within 21 days? If the answer is no, you're most of the way there.

A couple of things to know:
- He can't deduct for ordinary wear and tear, only for damage beyond that, unpaid rent, or cleaning to return the unit to its move-in condition.
- If he suddenly produces an itemized statement after your letter, it's late, and you can still dispute it — but it changes the conversation from "he kept it all" to "are these deductions legitimate."
- Keep everything in writing from now on. Don't phone him.

If you tell me the deposit amount and what, if anything, he said about the condition of the unit when you left, I'll help you tailor the demand letter.

Almost certainly not done for. What you're describing is a starter that's hungry, not dead.

The grey liquid is "hooch" — alcohol the yeast produced once they ran out of food. The nail-polish smell is acetone and other esters from the same starvation. Both are signs of a starter that's been neglected, and both go away with feeding. A month in the fridge is well within what a starter survives.

The only things that would mean it's actually gone: pink or orange streaks, fuzzy mould (any colour), or a smell that's rotten rather than sharp and chemical. If you've got any of those, bin it. Grey liquid and acetone is not that.

To bring it back:
1. Pour off the hooch (or stir it in if you want a more sour starter — either is fine).
2. Take about a tablespoon from below the surface; discard the rest.
3. Feed it at a high ratio — roughly 1 part starter to 5 parts flour to 5 parts water by weight — and leave it at room temperature.
4. Repeat every 12 hours or so. For the first day or two it may do very little. By day three or four it should start rising and smelling yeasty and sour again. Once it reliably doubles within 6–8 hours of a feed, it's back.

It may take a few days longer than that if your kitchen's cold. The pride was justified; it's a tough thing.

The last ten minutes falls apart because, from where they sit, the lesson is already over and you're the only one who hasn't acknowledged it. "Stay seated until the bell" is a rule about posture; it doesn't give them anything to do, so it decays. What tends to hold is making the last ten minutes a part of the lesson that has its own shape and its own stakes — and then letting them pack up on your signal, not theirs.

A structure that works for a lot of people:

1. Decide the sequence and make it visible every lesson. Something like: 12 minutes to go — exit task, seated. 4 minutes to go — pack up on your word. Then dismissal by rows or by table when they're standing quietly. Put the timings on the board. The key move is that packing up is something you grant, so there's no point doing it early.

2. The exit task has to matter. Three questions on today's content, on a slip or mini-whiteboard. You collect them, and you use them — tomorrow's starter is "here's what most of you got wrong yesterday." If it visibly feeds into something, it gets done. If it's just busywork, they'll clock that in a week, which is probably why the previous attempts lasted a week.

3. Control the door physically. You stand at it. Nobody leaves past you until their row is dismissed. This sounds obvious but it changes the geometry: the door is yours, not theirs.

4. Dismissal as a reward, not a right. The row that's packed quietly and standing behind chairs goes first. The last row out is the one still chatting. It takes a couple of weeks for the message to land that the order isn't random.

5. Friday period 5 specifically. Lower the content load in the last ten and raise the structure. A quick-fire quiz with a tiny stake — team points, first out — gives them the energy release they're going to have anyway, inside a format you run. Fighting a Friday afternoon for silent seated work is a losing battle; channelling it isn't.

The reason it only lasts a week each time is probably that the rule is restated and then not enforced consistently once the novelty passes, and the kids are measuring that very precisely. So pick a structure you can actually run every single lesson, including on the days you're tired, and make it boringly identical. The first fortnight is the expensive bit; after that it's just what happens.

If you tell me roughly what the current lesson ending looks like — do you have a plenary at all, do they leave on the bell or on you — I can suggest a specific script for the first week.

You're not doing anything unreasonable, but there's one thing in the setup that's probably working against you, and it isn't your consistency.

At ten weeks a collie cross is a baby. Being alone in a crate at night is new, frightening, and he can't yet hold his bladder all night anyway. Crying isn't naughtiness; it's "I'm alone and I don't know where you are." The advice to "be consistent" is sound, but it matters what you're being consistent with. Right now the consistent pattern he's learning is: cry for a long time, and eventually someone comes and stays. So he's getting better at crying for a long time. That's why it's lengthening, not shortening.

What tends to work better, in rough order of impact:

1. Move the crate into your bedroom, next to the bed, for now. This single change resolves most of it for most puppies. He can hear and smell you, you can put a hand down to the crate, and you'll hear him if he genuinely needs the toilet. You can move the crate out of the bedroom gradually in a few weeks once he's settled. There's no rule that a puppy has to sleep alone from day one, and most trainers now advise against it.

2. Make sure he's actually tired and empty. A proper play session and a toilet trip right before bed, and lift the water bowl an hour or so before. At ten weeks expect at least one night toilet trip — carry him out, no talking, no play, back in the crate.

3. Build crate love in the daytime. Feed him in it with the door open. Throw treats in. Chews in there. Short, calm closed-door sessions while you're in the room. Right now the crate may mean "the thing that happens when I'm abandoned." You want it to mean "my spot."

4. Consider something warm and something that smells of you — a worn t-shirt, a snuggle puppy toy with a heartbeat, or a covered crate so it feels like a den.

5. If he cries once he's in the bedroom crate, a calm word or a hand on the crate is fine. You're not aiming for silent indifference; you're aiming for "you're safe, I'm here, go to sleep," with the going-in-and-sitting-for-hours part removed because it's no longer needed.

One quick check: is he also ok in the crate during the day with you around, or does he panic whenever the door shuts? If it's the latter, that points to crate aversion specifically rather than nighttime loneliness, and the daytime work in step 3 is the priority.

You'll likely see a big change within a few nights of moving him. It feels like a step backwards; it's the fastest route forwards.

You've done the right things. The problem isn't that you haven't done enough — it's that a verbal request gets "we'll keep an eye on him," and a written one starts a legal clock. That's the change to make this week.

**Put the evaluation request in writing.** Under federal law (IDEA) and Ohio's rules, once you request an evaluation for a suspected disability in writing, the district has 30 days to either get your consent to evaluate or give you written notice explaining why they're refusing. If they evaluate, they have 60 days from your consent to complete it and meet with you. "Let's keep watching" is no longer an option once the letter exists. Send it to the principal and the school's special education coordinator (not just the teacher), by email so it's dated, and keep a copy. Something like:

"I am requesting a full and individual evaluation of my son, [name], grade 3 at [school], for special education eligibility under IDEA. I am concerned about his reading, including [specific: he cannot read a full sentence independently; this has been raised at conferences since kindergarten]. Please send me the consent form and the written notice required by Ohio Operating Standards. I understand the district has 30 days to respond to this request. Thank you."

**Two Ohio-specific things to ask about in the same email:**
- Ohio's Third Grade Reading Guarantee requires schools to assess every K-3 student and put any student who's not on track on a Reading Improvement and Monitoring Plan (RIMP). Ask whether he has one, and for a copy. If he's in third grade and can't read a sentence, he should.
- Ohio's dyslexia law requires schools to screen K-3 students for dyslexia. Ask for his screening results and what tier of intervention he's receiving. If the teacher's answer has been "late bloomer" since kindergarten, there may be no screening data at all, and that's worth knowing.

**If the district says no or stalls:** you can ask for an Independent Educational Evaluation at district expense, or get a private evaluation (a licensed psychologist or a university reading clinic; some are sliding-scale). The Ohio Coalition for the Education of Children with Disabilities (OCECD) has free parent advocates who know the process and can help you with the letter or the meeting.

One honest note: "late bloomer" is a real thing for some kids in kindergarten and first grade. It is not a plausible explanation for a third grader who can't read a sentence. You are not overreacting.

The awkwardness you're feeling is the thing that stops anyone bringing it up, which is exactly how six weeks go by. The fact that you noticed is the whole reason she might get a visit this week.

Two things, in order.

First, go round yourself, today or tomorrow. Not with a meal plan — just knock, see how she is, ask what she actually needs now. Six weeks after a hip op she may be mobile enough that meals aren't the thing anymore; it might be lifts to physio, someone to carry the shopping in, a bin taken out, or honestly just company. You'll come back from that with something concrete to ask for, which makes the group message much easier to write.

Second, the message. Nobody will mind being reminded — most of them will have had the same half-thought and felt the same awkwardness. Keep it warm, short, and specific, with no guilt in it:

"Hi all — I popped in to see [name] today. She's doing well and said to say thank you for all the meals earlier on. She's still not able to [drive / get to the shops / manage the stairs easily] so there are a couple of things that would really help over the next few weeks: [a lift to physio on Tuesday mornings, someone to pick up bits from the shop when they're going anyway, a visit for a cup of tea]. I've put a list here [link] — if you can take one, just add your name. No pressure, even one slot is a big help. Thanks everyone."

A few things that make it land:

- Leading with "she said thank you" lets people feel good about what they did rather than bad about what stopped.
- Specific, small asks get filled; "anyone able to help?" gets silence.
- A simple shared list (a Google Sheet, or even just reply-in-thread) means people don't have to coordinate through you.
- Don't mention that it fizzled. Everyone knows. Naming it only adds the guilt you're trying to avoid.

If you want to make it more durable this time, ask two or three people privately whether they'd be a regular — one visit a week, same day — rather than running an open rota. Small standing commitments survive; big enthusiastic rotas don't.

You're not being a nag. You're being the person who noticed.
