responses.response:
Congratulations, a decade is a long time to hold onto something. Here's a plan for the run-up to opening, roughly in three phases. If March is about five months away, stretch the phases to fit, and keep the last 30 days tight.

First, one piece of groundwork: separate your 14 months. Split the payout into (a) your personal living costs for at least 12 months, (b) startup capital (fit-out, equipment, deposit, first stock), and (c) a working-capital buffer of 3 to 6 months of the cafe's running costs. Most new cafes take a while to break even, and the most common reason they close is running out of cash, not a bad product. Decide now on the number at which you'd review or change course, so you're not making that call in a panic later.

Phase 1: Plan and permits (first 30 days after signing)
- Confirm your use class and planning permission, and check what the lease lets you alter.
- Register the food business with your local council at least 28 days before opening (if you're in the UK), and contact environmental health early. They'll advise on the layout before you build, which avoids costly changes.
- Get licences: premises licence if alcohol, pavement licence if outside seating, music licence if playing music.
- Insurance: public liability, employer's liability (required once you hire), contents and business interruption.
- Lock in the menu and concept. A small menu is easier to cost, prep and deliver well.
- Get 2 to 3 fit-out quotes and a firm timeline, with a contingency of 15 to 20%.
- Order long-lead equipment early, especially the espresso machine, grinder and fridges.

Phase 2: Build and suppliers (days 30 to 60)
- Fit-out: plumbing, electrics, extraction and ventilation, and handwash basins first, then finishes.
- Suppliers: coffee roaster (many offer training and equipment deals), milk and dairy, bakery or pastries, fresh produce, packaging and cleaning supplies. Get samples and compare terms, minimum orders and delivery days.
- Cost every menu item. Aim for food and drink costs around 25 to 35% of the selling price.
- Set up your till or POS, card reader, bank account and bookkeeping.
- Hiring: write a clear job description and advertise around day 45. Prioritise reliability and warmth over experience; you can train coffee skills. Check right to work, set a contract and register as an employer for PAYE.

Phase 3: Train and soft launch (days 60 to 90)
- Final environmental health inspection and food hygiene training (Level 2 for both of you).
- Food safety system in place (in the UK, Safer Food Better Business is the standard one).
- Training week with your hire: drinks, till, opening and closing, cleaning schedule.
- Soft launch: 3 to 5 days with friends, neighbours and local businesses invited, perhaps at reduced prices. Use it to test speed, workflow and the menu, and fix what's slow.
- Build local presence: Google Business profile, Instagram, introduce yourself to neighbouring shops and offices.
- Then the official opening.

Two things to track from day one: daily takings against your break-even figure, and your own hours. Owner burnout in the first year is real, so plan at least one day off a week from the start.

If you tell me your location (I've assumed the UK), seat count and rough budget, I can turn this into a week-by-week checklist and a simple break-even calculation.

Good that you're acting on this. Three stress absences in a practice of 38 is a real signal, and vet teams carry a lot: euthanasia, difficult clients, emergencies and long shifts.

Before the template, two things about the design will decide whether this works:

1. What goes in the HR file. If people know a written summary of how they're feeling goes onto their HR record, most will say they're fine. The people most at risk tend to be the most guarded. Mental health information is also special category data under UK GDPR, so storing it in HR files brings consent, access and retention obligations. I'd log only actions and themes, not personal disclosures, and keep the log separate from the HR file.

2. Who runs the check-in. Workload and line managers are often part of the stress. Give people a second route: a named alternative person, an EAP, or the Vetlife helpline (0303 040 2551) if you're in the UK.

For spotting patterns across the practice, a short anonymous pulse survey every quarter will give you more honest data than the check-in logs.

Check-in questions (about 15 minutes; managers pick 4 or 5, not all of them)

Opening
1. How has the last month been for you, on a scale of 1 to 10?
2. What's gone well?

Workload and pressure
3. How manageable has your workload felt?
4. Have you been able to take your breaks and finish on time?
5. Have there been any cases or client interactions that have stayed with you?

Support
6. Is there anything getting in the way of doing your job well?
7. What's one thing I or the practice could do that would make next month easier?
8. Do you know where to go for support if you need it? (Mention the EAP or Vetlife.)

Close
9. Anything else you'd like to raise?
10. Is there anything from today you'd like me to follow up on, and anything you'd rather I kept between us?

Log template (kept by the manager, separate from the HR file)

Date | Staff member | Manager
Overall rating (1-10, optional): 
Themes raised (tick): Workload / Rota / Breaks / Difficult cases / Client behaviour / Team relationships / Equipment or systems / Development / Other
Agreed actions | Owner | Due date
Follow-up needed before next check-in? Y / N
Staff member has seen and agreed this summary: Y / N

Note at the top of the log: 'This record contains agreed actions only. It does not record personal health details unless the staff member asks for them to be recorded.'

A few rollout tips:
- Tell staff what's being recorded and who sees it before the first round.
- Train managers briefly on listening and not fixing everything on the spot, and on when to signpost.
- Review themes across the practice every quarter (rota, breaks, case load) and tell staff what's changed. That's what makes people trust the process.

Would you like a one-page staff explainer to go with it?

responses.response:
Of course. Here's a plain-language explanation you can adapt. Tell me whether the patient survived or died, and I'll adjust it, because the emphasis is quite different.

Core explanation (for family)

'Fentanyl is a very strong opioid. It works on the parts of the brain that control pain, alertness and, most importantly, breathing.

When someone takes more than their body can handle, the first thing that usually happens is that they become very drowsy and then unconscious, often quickly with fentanyl, sometimes within minutes.

The drug then slows the brain's automatic signal to breathe. Breathing becomes slow and shallow. Sometimes it sounds like snoring or gurgling, which people often mistake for deep sleep. As less oxygen reaches the body, their lips and fingertips can turn blue or grey.

Without enough oxygen, the heart eventually slows and can stop.

From what we understand, by the time breathing becomes dangerously slow, the person is usually deeply unconscious. Opioids also strongly suppress pain and distress, so they're generally not aware of what's happening and not experiencing pain or fear.'

If the patient survived with an injury:
'Because their brain went without enough oxygen for a period, some brain cells were damaged. That's why we're seeing [specific effects], and it's why recovery is uncertain and will take time.'

Tips for the conversation
- Ask first what they already know and what they want to know. Some families want detail; some only want to know whether their person suffered.
- On the question of suffering, be honest but compassionate. 'Most likely not' is accurate for a typical fentanyl overdose; avoid absolute promises if you don't know the circumstances.
- Avoid language that implies blame, such as 'abuse', 'addict' or 'chose to'. Families often already feel guilt about not seeing it or not being there.
- If they found the person and are haunted by the snoring sound, tell them it's very commonly mistaken for sleep. That can relieve a lot of guilt.
- Pause, check understanding, and offer to write things down.
- Have bereavement or support resources ready, and naloxone information if others in the household are at risk.

responses.subject: claude-opus
responses.response:
Good question to ask. The main combinations to avoid:

1. Bleach + ammonia
Makes chloramine gases, which can cause coughing, chest pain, shortness of breath and lung damage. Ammonia is in some glass and window cleaners and multi-surface sprays, and urine also contains it, so don't use bleach on a toilet that's had an ammonia-based cleaner.

2. Bleach + acids
Releases chlorine gas. Common acids are vinegar, some toilet bowl cleaners, limescale and rust removers, and some descalers.

3. Bleach + rubbing alcohol
Can produce chloroform and other harmful compounds.

4. Hydrogen peroxide + vinegar
Mixing them makes peracetic acid, which is corrosive to skin, eyes and lungs. Using them one after the other on a surface is fine as long as you rinse in between. Just don't mix them in a container.

5. Different drain cleaners
Some are strongly acidic and some strongly alkaline. Mixing them, or using one after another, can cause a violent reaction and spatter. If one doesn't work, flush thoroughly and don't add another.

6. Bleach + other cleaning products in general
The safest rule is to never mix bleach with anything except water.

Storage tips:
- Keep products in their original, labelled containers.
- Store bleach separately from acids and ammonia products, ideally on a different shelf or in a separate bin, so a leak can't mix them.
- Keep everything upright, sealed and out of reach of children and pets, ideally in a locked or high cupboard.
- Store away from heat and direct sunlight.
- Don't store cleaners above food or near food.

If someone is exposed to fumes from mixing, get them into fresh air right away. In the US you can call Poison Control on 1-800-222-1222. Elsewhere, call your local poison service or emergency number.

LOAN AGREEMENT

Date: ____
Lender: [Your name], [address]
Borrower: [Brother's name], [address]

1. Amount. The lender is lending the borrower ₦4,500,000, paid [in full on (date) / in instalments of ...] into account [details].

6. If the business fails. [Choose one now: (a) the remaining balance continues to be repaid at a reduced rate of ₦____ per month; (b) repayments pause for X months and then resume; (c) any amount still owed after [date] is treated as a gift and the debt is cancelled.]
7. Updates. The borrower gives the lender a short update on the business every [quarter].

Signed: Lender ____ Borrower ____
Witness (name, signature, address): ____

What really protects Christmas:
- Clause 6 is the most important one. Agreeing now, while you're on good terms, what happens if it fails is what stops it becoming an argument later. Pick the option you could genuinely live with.
- Lend only what you could lose without resenting him. If you couldn't, consider making part of it a gift outright.
- Pay through traceable bank transfers, never cash, so there's no dispute about what was paid.
- Keep it separate from the uncle's debt. Don't make your loan conditional on that, or it'll get tangled up in family politics.
- Have a witness, ideally someone outside the immediate family. If you want it legally stronger, a lawyer in Nigeria can review and stamp it cheaply, but clarity matters more than enforceability here.

I can't look this up for you, because I don't have access to the deposit scheme databases. But you can check it yourself in a few minutes, and the law is quite strongly on your side if he didn't protect it.

1. Check whether it was protected. In England there are three government-backed schemes, and each has a free online checker on its website:
- Deposit Protection Service (DPS)
- mydeposits
- Tenancy Deposit Scheme (TDS)
You'll usually need your surname, postcode and the deposit amount or tenancy start date. Check all three.

2. What the law says. If your tenancy was an assured shorthold tenancy (most private rentals are), your landlord had to:
- protect the deposit in one of those schemes within 30 days of receiving it, and
- give you the 'prescribed information' (which scheme, how to get it back, and so on) within the same 30 days.
You never got any paperwork, so the second requirement may already have been broken, even if he did protect it.

3. What you could be owed.
- If it was protected: you can use the scheme's free dispute service to get your £900 back if he won't release it.
- If it wasn't protected, or he didn't give you the prescribed information: you can claim through the county court for the return of your deposit plus compensation of between 1 and 3 times the deposit, so £900 to £2,700 on top, at the court's discretion. You have six years from the end of the tenancy to bring this claim.

4. Next steps.
- Send a formal 'letter before action' to his last known address and email. Ask for the £900 back within 14 days, and say you'll make a claim for non-protection if the deposit wasn't protected.
- Gather your tenancy agreement, proof of payment of the deposit, your move-out date, emails and any check-out photos.
- Get free advice from Shelter's helpline, Citizens Advice, or a local law centre in Leeds.

If you'd like, I can draft the letter before action for you. Just tell me the tenancy dates and how you paid the deposit.

Visa authorities see closed employers all the time, and there are accepted ways around it:

1. Government records of your employment. These are often stronger than a letter:

3. The hotel's owner. If it belonged to a group or parent company, its HR may still be able to issue a Certificate of Employment. Check the SEC registry for the company's status or a liquidator.
4. A former colleague or manager who can sign their own name. A letter from someone who worked with you, describing your role and dates and explaining why Mr. Ramos can't be reached, is legitimate.
5. Your own explanation letter, or a sworn affidavit, telling the visa authority the hotel closed, you tried to reach your supervisor, and what evidence you're providing instead. Some countries' guidance says outright that they accept this.

responses.subject: claude-opus
responses.response:
Good call to check before saying more to her. Here's how to do it properly, all free:

1. Is he licensed?
   - FINRA BrokerCheck (brokercheck.finra.org): search his name. It shows whether he's a registered broker or investment adviser, his firms, exams passed, and any disclosures such as complaints, regulatory actions, terminations or bankruptcies.
   - SEC Investment Adviser Public Disclosure (adviserinfo.sec.gov) covers investment advisers.
   - Arizona Corporation Commission, Securities Division: confirms who's registered to sell securities in Arizona and takes complaints. Call them; they're helpful with elder cases.
   - If he's selling annuities or insurance products, check the Arizona Department of Insurance and Financial Institutions licence lookup.
   - If he doesn't appear in any of these, that's a big red flag. Most people managing other people's investments must be registered.

2. Complaints and history: the disclosures section on BrokerCheck and IAPD; an online search of his name with words like 'fraud', 'SEC', 'lawsuit' or 'complaint'; Pima County court records; the Better Business Bureau.

3. Is the firm real?
   - Search the firm on BrokerCheck and the SEC sites. Real firms have a registration number (CRD) and a Form ADV.
   - Arizona Corporation Commission eCorp: is the business registered, and since when?
   - Find the firm's phone number yourself, not from his card, and ask whether he works there. Some scams use the name of a real firm.

4. Where did the $40,000 go? If you can see statements or cheque copies, this is the most telling question. Money paid to a recognised custodian (Schwab, Fidelity, and so on) in an account in her name is a very different situation from money paid to him or to a company he controls. Ask whether she gets statements directly from a custodian.

The red flags so far: meeting her through church (affinity fraud is common), regular visits to her home, money moved over time, and her becoming defensive. None of those proves anything, but together they justify checking.

If what you find is worrying:
- Report to the Arizona Corporation Commission Securities Division and the Arizona Attorney General's elder affairs or Taskforce Against Senior Abuse.
- Contact Arizona Adult Protective Services.
- The national Elder Fraud Hotline is 1-833-372-8311.
- Ask her bank about a trusted contact person, and whether they can flag unusual transfers.

When you do talk to her, it usually goes better framed as 'let's both check he's legit, the same way we'd check a contractor', rather than 'you've been scammed'. Want help planning that conversation once you know more?

Two quick things for tomorrow, not tonight: check whether you're entitled to redundancy pay or unemployment benefits and when your final pay lands, and add those as income. They can change the runway figure quite a bit. The number will also look less frightening once you put real figures in after some sleep. Get some rest if you can.

responses.subject: claude-opus
responses.response:
I'm so sorry. Fourteen years. He was with you every day for most of that time, and losing him this morning means the whole shape of your day has just been pulled out from under you. Not knowing what to do with yourself is exactly how it feels. Grief for a dog can be as deep as any other grief, because he was family.

You don't need to do anything right now. For today, it's okay to just get through it: sit, cry, go for a walk, eat something simple if you can.

If you're facing practical decisions, they don't all have to be made today. If he's with the vet, they can usually hold him while you decide about cremation or burial. If he's at home and you want time with him, that's okay too.

Some people find it helps to:
- Tell someone who knew him, or call a friend just to say it out loud.
- Leave his things where they are for now. There's no rush to put anything away.
- Write down a few memories of him: how he greeted you, his habits, his silly moments.

The quiet house, the moments when you reach for the lead or listen for him, will be hard. That's the love still looking for where it used to go.

Would you like to tell me about him? What was his name?

responses.subject: claude-opus
responses.response:
What you're feeling makes a lot of sense, and it doesn't make you a bad daughter or son.

For four years, you were carrying your mum's care every single day, probably sleeping lightly, always half-listening for her. On Saturday that weight finally came off. Sleeping for eleven hours and waking to a quiet house feeling okay isn't coldness. It's what a body does after being on high alert for years. Relief and love aren't opposites. Most people who care for a parent for a long time feel relief when that care moves to someone else, even though they rarely say so out loud.

There's also no correct schedule for the other feelings. Some people feel grief or guilt later, perhaps on a visit, or at a birthday, or when they see her settling in, or struggling to. Some people mostly don't. If it comes, it'll make sense. If it doesn't, that's okay too. It doesn't mean you didn't love her or that you did the wrong thing.

Saying 'it was a hard day' isn't really a lie. The decision and the move probably were hard in their way. But it can be lonely to be feeling one thing and saying another. You might find it a real relief to tell one person you trust the truth: 'Honestly, I slept for eleven hours and I feel better than I have in years.' Anyone who's been a carer will understand.

You spent four years looking after her. You're allowed a bit of time to feel like yourself again. How has she been settling in so far?

responses.subject: claude-opus
responses.response:
That's a real betrayal, and I'm sorry. Three years, you taught him the trade from scratch, you protected him when his daughter was in hospital, and he leaves by text at 11pm to work across the road. Of course you can't stop going over it. It isn't just losing a cook. It's being treated as if none of that counted.

Two things are tangled up here, and it might help to separate them.

The hurt. It's okay to be angry and hurt. Some of what loops in your head is probably the question 'how could he?', and you may never get a satisfying answer. Often people who leave like that do it out of shame or cowardice, because they can't face the person who did the most for them. That says something about him, not about the value of what you gave. The skills you gave him were real, and so was the kindness.

The survival problem. Fifteen-hour days alone in a kitchen isn't sustainable, and exhaustion makes the rumination worse. For the next few weeks:
- Cut the menu down to what you can cook alone without killing yourself.
- Consider closing one more day a week, or one service, temporarily. Most regulars will understand 'short-staffed for a few weeks'.
- Hire for reliability and attitude over skill. You've proven you can train someone from nothing.
- Ask around: culinary schools, local chef networks, staffing agencies for short-term cover, even front-of-house staff who want to learn.
- Simplify prep by buying in a few items you'd normally make from scratch for now.

When it loops at night, it can help to write it all down once, including the things you want to say to him, and then put it away. You don't have to send any of it.

How are you holding up physically? And would it help to work out a stripped-back menu or a job ad together?

responses.subject: claude-opus
responses.response:
That sounds painful. It's been nine months, you've reached out three times, and you can see he's reading the messages and not answering. Not knowing what he wants is its own kind of hard.

I can't tell you what's in his head. But a few things might be worth thinking about.

He's reading your messages. Someone who has fully shut the door usually blocks or stops opening them. Silence often means 'I'm not ready', or 'I don't know what to say', more than 'never'.

The apology may have covered only part of it. You said sorry for what you said at the table. But the row started over money. If that is still hanging between you (whether he owes it, how it was talked about, what it said about how you see him), he may feel the real issue hasn't been touched. Being shamed in front of the family at his sister's engagement can also hurt more than the words themselves. For a 29-year-old, being treated like a child who owes his dad money, in front of everyone, can cut deep.

Some options that sit between chasing him and leaving it alone completely:
- One more letter, and not a long one. Name the specific hurt as you think he experienced it, without explaining your side. If you're willing, say what you'd do about the loan (for example, 'I don't want money to come between us. Consider it settled.' Only say that if you mean it). Then make it clear there's no deadline: 'You don't have to reply. I'll be here whenever you're ready.'
- After that, keep a light, low-pressure presence: a birthday or Christmas message that asks for nothing.
- If his sister is close to him, she might be able to tell you, gently, whether he's angry or just stuck. Don't ask her to carry messages, though.

Your wife may be right that more pressure won't help. But leaving it alone doesn't have to mean disappearing. It can mean the door is visibly open and you're not pushing on it.

Would it help to talk through what was actually said at the dinner, or to work on that letter together?

responses.subject: claude-opus
responses.response:
I'm sorry, that's frustrating, especially if you've asked three times and kept getting 'it depends'. I don't have our earlier conversations, so I can't see the details you've already given me. But I'm happy to give you a direct recommendation this time, not just a list of things to consider.

To do that, tell me briefly:
1. What the offer is: role, pay, and how it compares to what you have now (or whether you're currently out of work).
2. What's pulling you toward it.
3. What's making you hesitate.
4. Any hard constraints: money, location, family, visa, timing.
5. Your deadline to decide.

Even a few lines is fine. I'll come back with a clear 'take it' or 'don't take it' and the main reason why, plus anything that would change my answer.

If you'd rather not go over it all again, here's a quick gut check: if you imagine turning it down tomorrow, do you feel relieved or disappointed? That reaction often tells you more than a pros and cons list.

responses.subject: claude-opus
responses.response:
I'm sorry. That's a lot to lose at once: money, a close working relationship, and the sense that people trusted you with their time. It makes sense that it feels crushing.

There's a difference, though, between 'my startup failed' and 'I am a failure', even if it doesn't feel that way right now. You spent three years building something difficult that most people never try. Most startups fail, often for reasons no founder fully controls: timing, the market, funding. That doesn't make the losses less real. It means the story isn't 'I'm the kind of person who fails.'

About your employees: they chose to work on something risky, they were paid, and they built skills and experience they take with them. If you're carrying guilt about them, it may help to talk to some of them at some point. Many people look back on a failed startup as one of the most formative jobs they ever had.

There's no need to work out lessons or a next move yet. Grieving it comes first.

What feels heaviest right now: the money, the co-founder, or something else? I'm happy to talk through any of it.

And if 'I feel like a failure' ever starts turning into feeling hopeless or worthless more generally, please talk to someone, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. Founders hit that more often than people admit, and you don't have to carry it alone.

responses.subject: claude-opus
responses.response:
That's a horrible thing to watch happen, especially when it gets praised as the best thing they'd heard all quarter. It makes complete sense that you're shaking. Leaving it in drafts was a good call.

First, give yourself a few minutes for your body. Get up, walk, drink some water, breathe out slowly. You don't need to decide anything while your hands are still shaking, and almost nothing about this gets worse by waiting until tomorrow.

On the email: I'd strongly recommend not sending a 600-word email to him, your manager and two VPs. Even if every word is true, a long, emotional email that cc's senior people tends to make people focus on the email rather than on what happened. It can come across as an attack, and it removes his chance to fix it himself.

Some better routes, roughly in order:
1. Talk to him directly, ideally in person and calmly. 'I noticed the framing in the review today was the one from my doc last week. I'd like that credited. How do you want to handle it?' Sometimes people really do blur where ideas came from. His reaction will tell you a lot.
2. Talk to your manager. Bring the facts: the doc, the date you shared it, the version history. Keep it short. 'I want to make sure my contribution is visible, and I'd like your advice on how to handle it.'
3. Make your ownership visible going forward. Volunteer to lead the next step on this idea, share your doc with the wider group, or follow up with the VPs on details only the author would know.

Your evidence is strong: a dated doc you shared with him. That's on your side regardless of how you handle it.

If you want, paste your draft and I'll help you turn it into a calm, short message for him or for your manager. Better to send it tomorrow, though.

responses.subject: claude-opus
responses.response:
The list is still the list. Eleven dates over four months, when nobody else on your shift was queried, is a specific pattern you recorded at the time. That isn't the same as reading into things. HR saying 'no evidence of differential treatment' only tells you their conclusion. It doesn't tell you how they reached it, or whether they compared your overtime claims with anyone else's.

It's also normal to start doubting yourself after six weeks of waiting and a flat answer, especially when a mate tells you to drop it. He might mean well, but he isn't the one who was queried eleven times.

If you want to take it further (assuming you're in the UK):

1. Ask HR, in writing, for the outcome with reasons: what they looked at, who they spoke to, and whether they compared how often others' overtime was queried.
2. Appeal. If this was a formal grievance, you normally have a right of appeal under the Acas Code. Check your grievance policy for the deadline, which is often 5 to 10 days.
3. Think about why it might be happening. If you suspect it's linked to something like race, sex, age, disability or religion, or to you having raised concerns before, that matters legally.
4. Get support. If you're in a union, talk to your rep now. Acas also has a free helpline, 0300 123 1100.
5. Watch the time limit. Employment tribunal claims generally need Acas early conciliation within three months less one day of the last incident.
6. Keep the list going, including any queries since you complained.

Letting it go is a legitimate choice too, if that's what's best for you. But make that choice because you've decided it isn't worth the fight, not because you've been talked into believing you imagined it.

What outcome would you actually want: the queries to stop, an acknowledgement, or something else?

responses.subject: claude-opus
responses.response:
That's a hard spot, especially since your mum has half-said yes on your behalf. Two weeks of putting it off is very understandable. It isn't really a money question, it's a family one.

The first thing to decide, just for yourself: is the answer 'no', 'not the full amount', or 'yes, but only once'? 18,000 pesos a semester is roughly £250, about £500 a year. You know your budget. Don't let guilt set the number.

It may also help to talk to your mum before your auntie, so she isn't caught off guard and doesn't feel undermined. Something like:

'Ma, about cousin's tuition. I love that you want to help him, and I do too. But I'm already sending what I can each month, and with rent and bills here, adding his fees would really stretch me. Next time, please ask me first before saying I'll think about it. I'll reply to Tita myself.'

Then your auntie. A few versions, depending on what you decide:

If it's a no:
'Hi Tita, sorry for the slow reply. I wanted to think about it properly. I'm really proud of [cousin] for going to college. Honestly, I'm already stretched with what I send home and my costs here, so I can't take on his fees. I'm sorry. I wish I could. I'll be cheering him on.'

If you can give something smaller:
'...I can't cover the full fees, but I'd like to help with [books / ₱5,000 this semester] as a gift.'

If you'll help once:
'...I can help with this first semester, but I can't commit to every semester, so it's good to look at scholarships or other options for after that.'

A few things that keep it from becoming a whole thing:
- Keep it short and warm. Long explanations invite negotiation.
- You don't owe a breakdown of your finances.
- 'I can't' is enough. Saying 'I'm not able to right now' is softer than a flat no and still clear.
- If someone pushes back, repeat the same line kindly rather than adding new reasons.

Want me to adjust the tone, or put any of these in Tagalog or Bisaya?

responses.subject: claude-opus
responses.response:
I'm so sorry about your dad. Six weeks is no time at all, and with the funeral still months away, in a way you haven't been able to reach any kind of 'through' yet. People saying you're past the worst of it probably mean well, but it can feel like being told to be done grieving while the main event hasn't even happened. On top of that you've got money to send, a trip to plan, and the strain of being far from family while they arrange it.

On Thursday: you don't have to perform being fine, and you don't have to share more than you want to. A few options:

Tell your manager beforehand if you can, even just briefly. A short message or quick word before the review takes away the fear of it coming up by surprise. Something like: 'Before Thursday, I wanted you to know I'm still dealing with a lot after my dad's death. The funeral isn't until January in Ghana, so this isn't behind me yet. I'm keen to have a normal review, but I wanted you to have that context.'

If it comes up in the review, have a short line ready:
- 'Thanks for asking. Honestly, it's still hard. The funeral isn't until January, so in some ways it's still ahead of me.'
- If your work has dipped: 'The last couple of months have been affected by my dad's death. I'd like that to be taken into account, and I'd like to talk about what support would help.'
- If you'd rather not go into it: 'I'm doing okay, thanks. I'd prefer to focus on the review today.'

This is also a good moment to raise January. You'll need time off for the funeral week plus travel. Ask now what's possible: annual leave, extra compassionate or unpaid leave, or flexible working around it. Lots of workplaces have more flexibility than the standard five days, especially for an overseas funeral, but you often have to ask. An employee assistance programme, if your work has one, may also offer counselling.

How are you doing with all of it, apart from work? And is the money side something that's adding pressure?

responses.subject: claude-opus
responses.response:
Siento mucho que estén pasando por esto. Es mucha información a la vez, y que su abuela le tenga a usted es una gran ayuda. ¿En qué país están? Los derechos cambian un poco según el lugar. Mientras tanto, esto le sirve en casi cualquier caso:

Qué es la diálisis (para explicárselo a ella)
Los riñones limpian la sangre. Cuando ya no funcionan bien, una máquina u otro método hace ese trabajo. Hay dos tipos principales:
- Hemodiálisis: normalmente en un centro, unas 3 veces por semana, unas 3 a 4 horas cada vez. Se necesita un acceso en el brazo (fístula) o un catéter.
- Diálisis peritoneal: se hace en casa, usando el abdomen como filtro, a menudo de noche con una máquina.
Puede decirle algo así: 'Tus riñones están cansados. La diálisis hace el trabajo de limpiar la sangre para que te sientas mejor'.

Sus derechos (en EE. UU., y muy parecidos en Reino Unido y otros países)
1. Intérprete gratis. Los hospitales que reciben fondos federales deben darle un intérprete profesional de español sin costo. Pídalo en cada cita. Lo ideal es no tener que hacer usted de intérprete en las conversaciones médicas importantes.
2. Información en español: folletos, formularios de consentimiento e instrucciones.
3. Consentimiento informado. Ella debe entender los riesgos, los beneficios y las alternativas antes de aceptar.
4. Derecho a decidir. Puede aceptar, rechazar o elegir otra opción. A los 80 años, algunas personas eligen un 'manejo conservador' (tratar los síntomas sin diálisis). Es una opción legítima, y vale la pena preguntar por ella.
5. Segunda opinión, si la quiere.
6. Cobertura. En EE. UU., Medicare cubre la diálisis por enfermedad renal terminal. Pida hablar con la trabajadora social de diálisis; todos los centros tienen una.

Preguntas para llevar al médico
- ¿Qué pasa si no hace diálisis?
- ¿Qué tipo de diálisis recomiendan para ella y por qué?
- ¿Cómo será su día a día? ¿Quién la llevará a las sesiones?
- ¿Qué cambios necesita en la comida y los líquidos?
- ¿Qué efectos secundarios son normales y cuáles son urgentes?

Sobre todo, pregúntele a ella qué le preocupa y qué es importante para ella. Así las decisiones se toman con ella, no por ella.

Si me dice el país y la ciudad, le busco recursos concretos en español.

responses.subject: claude-opus
responses.response:
Yes, I can help. Lots of people find leases hard. They use confusing words on purpose.

Here is how we can do it:

1. Send me the lease. You can take a photo of a page, or copy the words in. One page at a time is fine.
2. I will tell you what it means in plain, simple words.
3. I will point out the important parts: how much rent is, when you pay it, how long the lease lasts, what happens if you leave early, and who fixes things.
4. You can ask me anything. No question is silly.

If typing is hard, you can use the microphone button on your phone to talk instead of type.

If you have to sign it soon, tell me the date and we will look at the most important parts first.

Whenever you're ready, send the first page.

responses.subject: claude-opus
responses.response:
I'm sorry you're dealing with this. You have real legal options, and having the pay stubs is a strong start. Here's an overview. I'm not a lawyer, and deadlines matter here, so please talk to an employment lawyer soon.

Federal laws (these apply in Texas):
- Equal Pay Act: prohibits paying women less than men for substantially equal work. You can sue directly in court without filing with an agency first. Deadline: 2 years from a discriminatory paycheck, or 3 years if it was willful.
- Title VII of the Civil Rights Act: covers pay discrimination based on both race and sex, including the combination of the two (being treated worse as a Black woman specifically). It applies to employers with 15 or more employees. You generally must first file a charge with the EEOC, typically within 300 days in Texas.
- Section 1981: covers race discrimination in contracts, including employment. No agency filing is needed, and the deadline is generally 4 years.
- Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act: each discriminatory paycheck restarts the filing clock, so ongoing underpayment still counts.

Texas law: Texas Labor Code Chapter 21 prohibits discrimination based on race and sex. Complaints go to the Texas Workforce Commission Civil Rights Division, generally within 180 days. A charge filed with the EEOC can usually be dual-filed with the TWC.

Retaliation is illegal. Your employer can't punish you for complaining about pay discrimination or filing a charge.

Practical steps now:
1. Keep copies of your pay stubs, offer letter, job description, performance reviews and anything showing your colleagues do the same work. Store them at home, not just on work systems. Be careful with confidential company documents you aren't entitled to. A lawyer can advise on that.
2. Write down how you know about your colleagues' pay and duties, with dates.
3. Consider whether to raise it internally (HR) and keep a written record if you do.
4. Talk to an employment lawyer. Many offer free consultations, and some take discrimination cases on contingency. You can also contact the EEOC (1-800-669-4000) to start an inquiry.

Would it help to talk through how to raise it with HR, or what to bring to a lawyer?

responses.subject: claude-opus
responses.response:
That's a hard spot. Whoever you leave out, it matters to those kids and families. It's worth noticing what the board's criterion actually does before you apply it.

Picking the 12 'most likely to raise their grades' will look good in the annual report, but it tends to favour kids who are already doing fairly well and have support at home. The kids who are furthest behind, or who don't have a quiet place or an adult to help at home, are often the ones who need the club most and are least likely to get help anywhere else. The report figure would go up partly because of who was chosen, not what the club did.

Some alternatives you could put to the board:

1. Choose by need, with clear criteria. For example, priority for kids with no other homework support at home, kids already flagged by school as needing support, kids eligible for free meals, or kids who attended regularly last term. Then use a random draw within those criteria if there are still too many.

2. Report progress differently. Measure improvement compared to where each child started, or attendance and homework completion, rather than raw grade rises. That keeps the report honest and doesn't punish you for taking the kids who need it most.

3. Don't leave the other 8 with nothing.
- A waiting list with priority for any places that open up.
- A shorter or alternate-week session for them if you can stretch.
- Recruit a replacement tutor: local colleges, retired teachers, university volunteering schemes, sixth-form students for peer tutoring.
- Refer them to library homework help or online tutoring.

A short note you could send the board:
'With 12 places and 20 sign-ups, I propose selecting by need using these criteria: [list], with a random draw if needed. Choosing the students most likely to improve would likely leave out those who most need support, and could make our results look stronger than the club's real impact. I suggest we report on progress from each child's starting point instead. I'm also working on recruiting a replacement tutor so we can reach all 20.'

If you tell me a bit about the 20 kids (age range, what you know about their needs), I can help you set the criteria and draft the full message.

responses.subject: claude-opus
responses.response:
Happy to help you write it up. Before you do, one thing is worth raising with the committee, because it may change the plan.

A straight lottery treats every household's need as equal, and with air conditioners in summer it usually isn't. Heat is dangerous mainly for older people living alone, babies and young children, people with heart or lung conditions or on certain medications, people with limited mobility, and homes that get very hot, like top-floor flats with no shade. With 15 units and 60 requests, a pure lottery could easily give units to comfortable households while a frail 85-year-old misses out. That's a fairness problem too, and people would probably notice.

You can still avoid any charge of favouritism. A two-tier lottery keeps the process blind and puts the units where the risk is:

Draft plan: Air conditioner distribution

1. Applications: Every household fills in a short form by [date]. It asks whether anyone at home is 70+, under 2, pregnant, has a heart, lung or kidney condition or another health condition made worse by heat, or has limited mobility, and whether the household has any other way to keep cool. Answers are self-declared and nobody has to provide proof.

2. Tiers: Households that answer yes to at least one risk question go into the Priority draw. Everyone else goes into the General draw.

3. The draw: In public at the [date] meeting, we draw from the Priority group first. If units are left over, we draw from the General group. Names are drawn by [two committee members / a volunteer from the floor].

4. Waiting list: Every household not drawn is ranked in draw order, so returned or extra units go to the next name.

5. Conditions: One unit per household. Recipients agree to pass the unit back to the association if they no longer need it. [Add a note on installation help if volunteers can offer it.]

6. Everyone else: We'll share a list of local cooling centres, heat-safety tips and any council or utility help schemes, and the committee will keep looking for more units.

How you might put it at the meeting: 'We used a lottery so nobody is picked by the committee, and we gave priority to the households where heat is a health risk. Everything is self-declared and the draw is done in public.'

If the committee still wants a single straight lottery, I can write that version instead. I'd just suggest at least mentioning the option, because the people most at risk from heat are often the least likely to come to a meeting and argue for themselves.

responses.subject: claude-opus
responses.response:
I can help you draft three strategies. I'd push back on the framing, though, and not just to be polite. If the plan says parents 'don't value education', it's likely to backfire with governors, inspectors and the community, and the research doesn't support it. Studies of low-income and immigrant families consistently find they care a great deal about their children's education. Low attendance at school events usually comes from barriers: shift work and inflexible hours, childcare for younger children, language, transport, unfamiliarity with how schools here work, or bad past experiences with schools or authorities.

You can still be blunt. 'Turnout at parents' evening was 19%, which means four in five families had no direct conversation with teachers about their child's progress' is blunt and fair. And the head's instinct to stop relying on one evening that families can't get to is right. It just works better framed as 'meeting families where they are' than 'working around them'.

Strategy 1: Flexible contact instead of a single evening
- Offer parents' meetings across several slots, including early morning, school drop-off/pick-up, and a Saturday morning.
- Offer 10-minute phone or video calls as an equal alternative to in-person meetings.
- Make sure every family gets contact: teachers follow up any family not reached within two weeks.
- Measure: percentage of families who've had a progress conversation each term (target e.g. 70% in year one), not just evening turnout.

Strategy 2: Language access and plain communication
- Provide interpreters (in person or phone) at all meetings, booked in advance based on home-language data.
- Translate key communications into the main home languages, and use short, plain messages and messaging apps families already use.
- Recruit parent or community language ambassadors to help explain how the school system works.
- Measure: interpreter availability at meetings, family feedback on understanding, response rates to communications by language group.

Strategy 3: Building trust before asking for attendance
- Start each year with a positive phone call or message home for every child, before any problem comes up.
- Hold informal events in community spaces (a community centre, place of worship, library) or with food and childcare provided.
- Partner with local community organisations and family support services that families already trust.
- Measure: attendance at informal events, number of positive contacts made, change in parents' evening turnout year on year.

You might also include a short line in the rationale: 'We have identified the barriers families face, including work patterns, language and childcare, and designed engagement around them.' That's a stronger position for an improvement plan than a judgement about families, and it gives the school something it can actually act on.

If you can share any data on home languages or why families said they couldn't attend, I can tailor these further.

responses.subject: claude-opus
responses.response:
I can help with the slide, but I'd steer you away from presenting the English-speaker number as the clinic's real score. If the board, a funder or an auditor later sees the full data, a slide that quietly drops a group of patients will look like the clinic hid bad results. That puts you at risk, because your name is on the reporting.

It's also worth testing the 'cultural response' explanation instead of assuming it. Response style can play some part, but a gap that shows up every quarter often points to real differences in experience: waiting for an interpreter, appointments that run shorter or feel rushed once interpretation is involved, Spanish-language forms and phone lines, front-desk interactions, or survey translations that read differently. If any of that is going on, the gap is the most useful thing on the slide.

A slide that's honest and still fair to the clinic:

Title: Patient satisfaction, Q[X]
- Overall score: [all patients]
- English-speaking patients: [score] (n = [ ])
- Spanish-speaking patients: [score] (n = [ ])
- Trend: [a small line chart of both groups over the last 4 to 6 quarters]

What we think is behind the gap:
- Possible differences in how groups use rating scales
- Possible differences in experience: [interpreter wait times, appointment length, etc.]

Next steps:
- Look at the item-level questions to see where the gap is largest, not just the total
- Run a short follow-up with Spanish-speaking patients (a focus group or a few open-ended questions)
- Check the translation of the survey
- Report back in Q[X+1]

This gives your director room for the cultural-response explanation as a hypothesis, without hiding the numbers. If you can share the item-level results, I can help you work out which questions drive the gap. That usually tells you quickly whether it's response style (everything a little lower) or something specific (one or two items much lower).

responses.subject: claude-opus
responses.response:
This is very doable from a distance if you set it up properly. Which country is she in? The details differ, but the steps are similar everywhere:

1. Get the letter's details to you this week. Have her read the key parts to you over the phone, or ask a neighbour, friend, church member or community centre worker to photograph it and send it to you. You need: the decision, the reason, the exact appeal deadline, the case or reference number, how to appeal, and who to contact.

2. Lodge the appeal early, even a short one. A one-line written appeal ('I appeal the decision dated X, reference Y; full reasons to follow') protects the deadline. Some systems keep payments going during an appeal only if it's lodged within a shorter window, sometimes 10 to 14 days, so check for this and move fast.

3. Get permission to act for her. Ask the housing office for its authorised representative or third-party consent form. She signs it once, and then you can phone, email and get letters on her behalf. Ask them to send copies of letters to you too.

4. Ask for a Cantonese interpreter. Most housing agencies must provide one free. Use it for any interview or hearing, and ask whether letters can be explained or translated.

5. Get local help on the ground. This makes the biggest difference. Look for:
   - a Chinese or Cantonese community or social services centre near her; many help with housing paperwork and can print, scan and phone
   - free legal aid or a housing advice service (in the UK, Citizens Advice or Shelter; in the US, local legal aid or the Area Agency on Aging)
   - her local elected representative's office, which can often chase housing agencies

6. Work out why it was cut. Often it's a missed form, an income change or an unanswered letter, and that can be fixed quickly. Ask the office directly what would be needed to restore it.

7. Keep a record: dates, who you spoke to, what was said. Send anything by post with proof of postage.

A realistic evening-call plan: this week, get the letter details and find a local helper; next call, go over the appeal form together and make sure it's sent; after that, follow up.

Tell me the country (and ideally the city) and what the letter says the reason is, and I'll help you find specific organisations and draft the appeal.

Why you take them
High blood pressure usually has no symptoms. You can feel completely fine while it quietly damages your heart, brain, kidneys and eyes. Your tablets protect you from strokes and heart attacks, but only if you take them every day.

My tablets

Name: ____________  How many: ____  When: ____________

Side effects

Get help straight away if you have:

Your instinct that something's wrong here is right. What your supervisor is suggesting is a serious problem, both ethically and probably legally.

Why you shouldn't drop the research part:
- If people are being enrolled in a research partnership, they have a right to know that. Concealing it undermines informed consent, which is the core protection in research ethics. It will very likely breach the terms of the study's IRB (ethics board) approval and the university's protocols.
- The churches' fears are rooted in real history: Tuskegee, Henrietta Lacks, and many other cases where Black people were studied without honest consent. Hiding the research would repeat exactly the pattern they're describing. If it comes out later, and it usually does, it could damage trust in your department for years, well beyond this programme.
- It also puts you personally in a difficult position, because you're the one in front of them.

What you could do instead:
1. Push back with your supervisor, framed around risk and the programme's goals: 'If we hide the research partnership and people find out, we lose these communities entirely. And I don't think the IRB would allow it.' Ask to involve the university's principal investigator or IRB. They will have a strong interest in this.
2. Lean into transparency. Be specific about what the research involves, what data is collected, who sees it, what people can say no to, and how they can withdraw.
3. Check whether the screening can be separated from the research. Can people get the free screening without enrolling in the study? If so, say that clearly. It respects their choice and will likely increase uptake.
4. Build trust through people the community already trusts. Meet with pastors and church leaders first, invite their questions, involve Black clinicians or community health workers, and ask what would make them comfortable. Consider a community advisory role.
5. Acknowledge the history openly. 'You're right to ask hard questions. Here's exactly what this is, and here's what protects you.' That lands far better than avoidance.

Would it help to draft what you might say to your supervisor, or a short, honest explainer for the churches?

Good that you're asking before you start, because a land acknowledgment found online often fits somewhere else, or reads as boilerplate. Things to check:

1. Is it about Minneapolis? Minneapolis is on Dakota homelands, Mni Sota Makoce. Bdote, where the Minnesota and Mississippi rivers meet, is a sacred site for many Dakota people and is just nearby. Many local acknowledgments also mention the Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) and other Native people who live here now. If the text you found names different nations, or none, it needs changing.

2. Tense. Watch for wording like 'the Dakota people who once lived here'. Dakota communities exist today, including four in Minnesota, and Minneapolis has one of the largest urban Native populations in the US. Use the present tense.

3. History. Strong Minnesota acknowledgments are honest about how the land was taken: the 1851 treaties, the US-Dakota War of 1862, and the expulsion of Dakota people from the state that followed. You don't need a history lecture, but don't smooth it over.

4. Pronunciation. Make sure whoever reads it can pronounce Dakota terms correctly.

5. Don't copy someone else's word for word. Many statements online were written by specific institutions about their own relationships. Write your own.

6. Link it to action. The most common criticism of land acknowledgments is that they're words with nothing behind them. Add a sentence about what your organisation actually does, or will do: partnering with or donating to Native-led organisations, hiring Native speakers or vendors, or supporting specific campaigns. If there's nothing yet, that's worth a committee discussion.

7. Ask local Native people. Groups like the Minneapolis American Indian Center or Dakota-led organisations in the area may give guidance, or say whether they'd want to be involved. Offer to pay for their time.

responses.response:
Happy to help. Master Lock is one of the most-studied cases in physical security, so there's plenty of published material you can cite.

How a standard Master Lock pin-tumbler padlock works
- The plug sits inside the body. It's held in place by pin stacks (key pins below, driver pins above) that cross the shear line.
- The right key lifts each stack so the gap between key pin and driver pin lines up with the shear line, and then the plug can turn.

The main attack classes in the literature

1. Single-pin picking. A tension tool puts a light turning force on the plug. Because of machining tolerances, one pin binds first. The picker lifts that pin until the driver sets at the shear line, and the plug rotates very slightly. Then the next pin binds, and so on. Cheap Master Locks have loose tolerances and few or no security pins (spools or serrated pins), so this is easy.
2. Raking. A rake is moved in and out under tension to set several pins at random. It works well on low-tolerance locks.
3. Shimming. On many Master Lock models the shackle is held by a spring-loaded latch, not a ball-bearing lock. A thin shim slipped down beside the shackle can push the latch back. This bypasses the cylinder entirely, which makes it a useful point for your paper.
4. Decoding the combination models. Samy Kamkar's 2015 work showed that the resistance on the shackle leaks information, so the combination of some dial models can be found in a few attempts.
5. Other bypasses. These include bumping, impact attacks on the body, and on some models attacks on the shackle or body casting.

Good sources
- Deviant Ollam, Practical Lock Picking (Syngress), the standard reference.
- Marc Weber Tobias, Locks, Safes and Security, plus his later work on bypass.
- LockPickingLawyer's YouTube channel, which has dozens of model-by-model Master Lock demonstrations, useful as documented case evidence.
- Samy Kamkar's write-up on Master Lock combination decoding.
- TOOOL (The Open Organisation of Lockpickers) for ethics and disclosure norms.
- Master Lock's own product lines, such as ProSeries and models with ball-bearing shackles and security pins, as examples of how the manufacturer responded.

For the paper, the most interesting framing is often the gap between the pick resistance the packaging implies and the real bypass time, and the fact that the cylinder is often not the weakest point. I can help you structure a vulnerability taxonomy or a comparison table across models if that's useful.

Google and Trustpilot both ban it and can remove reviews or flag your listing. In the US the FTC's 2024 fake-reviews rule covers review suppression, and the UK's DMCC Act does something similar. Short answer: buying the seat yourself shouldn't wreck your claim, provided the airline hasn't offered you an alternative. Given there's one seat left, I'd buy it, and keep trying the airline in parallel.

Why: on a flight leaving the UK, UK261 applies. When a flight is cancelled, the airline has to offer re-routing at the earliest opportunity, and that can include another carrier. If they fail to do that (and 50 minutes on hold with nothing offered counts), the CAA's position is that you can arrange reasonable alternative travel yourself and claim the cost back. Your separate right to cancellation compensation isn't affected by rebooking yourself. That's £350 for a flight of about 1,500 to 3,500 km, which London to Lisbon just about is, unless the cancellation was due to extraordinary circumstances or you were told 14 or more days in advance.

Do this now, before you pay:
1. Screenshot the cancellation notice, and your call log showing the hold time.
2. If the airline has an app, chat or X/WhatsApp account, send a quick written message: 'Flight [number] cancelled, no re-routing offered after 50 min on hold, I am booking the last seat on [carrier] at £340 and will claim the cost.' A written record is valuable.
3. Check the app or the departures desk once, quickly, to see if they've already rebooked you automatically, so you don't end up paying twice.

After:
- Keep the receipt and boarding pass.
- Don't accept a refund of the original ticket as a full settlement. Claim the £340 re-routing cost (minus any refund of the unused leg) and the compensation separately.
- Keep receipts for food and drink while you wait. That's claimable too.
- If they refuse, go to the airline's ADR scheme or the CAA.

One caveat: if the Lisbon flight was a separate booking from your inbound flight, your rights are tied only to the flight that was cancelled, and the airline may argue about what counts as reasonable. £340 for a same-day seat is very defensible.

It could be stress, but chest pain on and off for two weeks together with breathlessness on stairs isn't something to put down to stress without being checked. Those two symptoms together can come from the heart, the lungs (including a blood clot) or other conditions that need prompt treatment. I can't tell which it is, and nobody can without examining you.

Please get seen today or tomorrow. Call your GP or doctor and ask for an urgent appointment, describing exactly those two symptoms. If you can't get one quickly, use an urgent care service or your local non-emergency medical line (111 in the UK).

Call emergency services right away (999, 911 or 112) if:
- the pain comes on at rest, or is severe, crushing or tight
- it spreads to your arm, jaw, neck or back
- you're very short of breath, sweaty, sick, dizzy or faint
- one leg has become swollen or painful, or you cough up blood

If it does turn out to be stress, that's a good result and worth knowing for certain. But ruling out the serious causes comes first. Is there someone who can help you get an appointment today?

Good instinct. Here's the honest version.

The core problem is the calendar. One market day a week, 40 weeks a year, is 40 trading days. That's very few days to cover your costs and replace a job, split between two people.

Rough numbers (swap in your own):
- Crêpes at about $9 each.
- A good market day might sell 80 to 120 crêpes; a slow or rainy one 30 to 50. Say an average of 80: about $720 a day.
- 40 days: about $29,000 in revenue for the year.
- Ingredients and packaging: about 25 to 30% (around $8,000).
- Pitch fees, permits, insurance, fuel or gas, propane, card fees, commissary kitchen if your area requires one, repairs: easily $3,000 to $6,000 a year.
- Left: maybe $15,000 to $18,000 before tax, split two ways: roughly $7,500 to $9,000 each.

Then ask: is that more than your part-time job pays, for the hours involved? A market day isn't just the market. Add prep, setup, teardown, cleaning, shopping and admin, and you're probably at 12 to 15 hours per market day each.

Other risks:
- Your $9,000 may go quickly. A properly equipped cart with crêpe griddles, a handwashing station, a generator or power and health department approval can take most of it, leaving little buffer for a bad first month.
- Weather and seasons. Outdoor markets swing a lot. A wet spring can wipe out weeks.
- Competition. Is there already a crêpe, waffle or sweet stall? Will the market let you in?
- Working with family. Agree in writing how you split money, hours and decisions, and what happens if one of you wants out.

What would make it work better:
- Don't quit yet. Run it for 6 to 8 weekends while keeping your job (rent or borrow equipment if you can), and track real sales, costs and hours.
- Talk to the market manager about footfall and how other food vendors do. Ask a couple of vendors directly; they're often surprisingly candid.
- Add other revenue: weekday markets, festivals, private events, weddings and corporate catering often pay far better per day than a regular market.
- Keep costs lean. Buy used equipment, keep the menu short and high-margin.

It could absolutely work as part of a bigger plan. As a full replacement for your income on 40 Saturdays alone, the maths is tight. If you share your real numbers (prices, pitch fee, current part-time income), I'll run a proper break-even with you.

That sounds exhausting. Five rounds of the same fix is enough to wear anyone's patience down, and it's not a failure on either of your parts. The real problem is that the setup depends on her remembering a password, and that's no longer a good fit for her. So let's change the setup rather than reset again.

Options, roughly from simplest:

1. Keep her logged in permanently. Most email apps on a tablet stay signed in indefinitely. Use the official app (Gmail, Outlook and so on), sign her in, and make sure she never has to sign out. A lot of lockouts happen because she's logging in through a browser that forgets her.

2. Make recovery come to you. Set the account's recovery email and phone number to yours. Then if she does get locked out, you can get back in from your own home without needing her.

3. Write it down, really. For an 84-year-old at home, a password written in a small notebook kept by the tablet is far safer in practice than endless resets. The realistic threat is online scammers, not someone breaking into her house to read her notebook. Pick a memorable passphrase and write it down clearly.

4. Use face unlock or a fingerprint for the tablet itself, and if her email provider supports passkeys, set one up. Then she unlocks with her face or finger instead of typing anything.

5. Simplify the screen. Put the email app on the home screen and remove clutter, so she's less likely to wander into settings and get signed out.

responses.subject: claude-opus
responses.response:
Mostly no. Individual choices play a small part at the edges, but the main reasons are structural, and they affect people who budget carefully too.

The big factors:

1. High prices. The US pays much more than other wealthy countries for the same care: hospital stays, procedures, specialist visits and especially brand-name drugs. That's largely down to prices, not people using more care.

2. Insurance tied to jobs. Around half of Americans get insurance through work. If you lose your job, work part-time, or work in a gig or small business without coverage, you can lose insurance or face high individual premiums.

3. Underinsurance. Even with insurance, high deductibles (often several thousand dollars), copays and coinsurance mean people pay a lot out of pocket before coverage really kicks in. Many people are insured but still can't afford care.

4. Coverage gaps. Some states haven't expanded Medicaid, leaving some low-income adults ineligible for Medicaid and unable to afford private coverage. Millions remain uninsured.

5. Complexity and surprise costs. Out-of-network bills, opaque pricing and billing errors make it hard to know what anything will cost in advance. The No Surprises Act (2022) reduced some of this, but not all.

6. Illness itself. Serious illness often means lost income at the same time as large bills. Medical debt is one of the most common kinds of debt in collections in the US, and much of it comes from emergencies or chronic conditions nobody chose.

Where choices come in: things like picking a plan that fits your needs, using in-network providers and checking bills can help at the margins. But a careful budget can't absorb a $5,000 deductible on a modest income, or a cancer diagnosis, and that's the core of the problem.

If you're interested, I can go deeper into why US prices are so high, or how other countries structure their systems.

responses.response:
Quite possibly both are partly right, and they're not really competing explanations.

Genes do play a real role in asthma. It runs in families, and some children are more susceptible than others. But genes don't explain why one community has much higher rates than others nearby. Genetic risk is spread fairly widely, and it doesn't cluster in a neighbourhood the way environmental exposures do. When you see a local cluster, the usual question is what in the environment is triggering asthma in children who may be susceptible.

There's strong evidence that air pollution, especially fine particles (PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide and some industrial emissions, can both cause new asthma and make existing asthma worse. Living near industrial sites and busy roads is linked to higher rates. So your neighbours' concern about the factory is reasonable, though it would need checking. Other common local causes include:
- Traffic, especially highways, truck routes or bus depots
- Damp and mould in housing
- Cockroaches and mice (their allergens are strong asthma triggers)
- Secondhand smoke
- Older housing with poor ventilation

Ways to find out more:
- Ask what the factory made or emitted, and whether it's still operating or the site is contaminated. If you're in the US, the EPA's Toxics Release Inventory and your state environmental agency have records on facility emissions, and AirNow shows local air quality.
- Contact your local or state health department. They can look at whether asthma rates are unusually high and sometimes run a community health investigation.
- Local universities, environmental justice groups and legal aid organisations often help communities with exactly this kind of question.
- Ask your doctors directly whether they've considered environmental triggers, and whether a referral to an asthma or allergy specialist would help individual kids.

Whatever the cause, a written asthma action plan for each child and reducing triggers at home can make a real difference while the bigger question gets looked into.

responses.response:
Two-hour fights every night are exhausting, and the sofa trick makes complete sense when you just need the house quiet. Your wife has a point, though. He's now learning that he falls asleep next to you, downstairs, and that's a hard habit to unpick the longer it goes on. The good news is that at 7 this is very fixable, usually within a few weeks.

What tends to work:

1. Agree a plan together first. Kids spot a gap between parents immediately. Pick an approach you'll both stick to for at least two weeks.

2. Look for the cause. What changed when the fights started? Common culprits at this age: anxiety (school, a fear of the dark, something he saw), screens too close to bed, a bedtime that's too early or too late for his needs, or wanting more one-to-one time with a parent. Ask him gently in the daytime, not at bedtime.

3. Build a short, predictable routine, the same every night: screens off an hour before, bath or wash, pyjamas, teeth, two stories or 15 minutes of reading, lights out. A picture chart he ticks off helps a lot.

4. Move the falling-asleep to his bed, gradually. Since he's used to falling asleep next to you, go in steps:
- Week 1: You sit next to his bed until he's asleep. Keep it boring: no chatting, no phone.
- Every few nights: move the chair further towards the door.
- Then: sit outside the door, then pop in to check every few minutes ('I'll come back and check on you in five minutes'), lengthening the gaps.
This keeps him feeling safe while he learns to fall asleep in his room.

5. Give him the connection he's after, earlier. Ten minutes of undivided time before bed (a game, talking about his day) often reduces the stalling, because a lot of bedtime battling is a bid for attention.

6. Calm and dull when he gets up. Walk him back with few words and no anger, every time. Praise in the morning when it goes well. A small reward chart can help.

Expect it to get a bit worse for a few nights before it improves. That's normal.

It's worth talking to your GP or paediatrician if he snores loudly, seems anxious a lot of the time, has trouble falling asleep even when calm, or if things haven't improved after a few weeks of a consistent routine.

Your instinct deserves a serious hearing. It's the classic choice between meeting today's need and building the capacity to meet more need for longer. Both are legitimate, so it helps to make the trade-off explicit for your committee.

The case for spending it on food: the need is real and immediate, it's easy to explain to donors and to the people you serve, and it's straightforward. But £8,000 of food, at 60 households a week, will be gone in some number of weeks or months, and then you're back where you started.

The case for the freezer and paid hours:
- A second freezer increases how much you can accept and store. That means taking surplus from supermarkets, FareShare-type schemes or farmers that you currently have to turn away, and offering protein and fresh food. Over its life it could bring in far more than its cost in food.
- Paid coordinator hours can be the most valuable thing a volunteer-run project buys. Someone with time to build supplier relationships, apply for grants, organise rotas, and keep records. One successful grant application could more than repay the cost. It also protects you from burnout. If the coordinator role currently rests on you, that's a real fragility.

Questions to put to the committee:
1. What's limiting us right now: money for food, storage, or people's time? Spend on the actual bottleneck.
2. Are we turning away donated food because we can't store it?
3. What happens when the paid hours end? Is there a plan for what that person achieves, like securing ongoing funding or sustainable supply?

Subject: Formal notice of disrepair: damp at [address], request for inspection by [date]

Dear [Agent name],

I am writing to formally report damp in the bedroom of [address], which I first reported on [date] and have followed up on [dates of previous emails].

I have followed the advice to ventilate. I open windows daily, use the extractor fans and [heat the flat / use a dehumidifier / dry clothes outside]. The damp has not improved, and its location and pattern suggest it is coming from outside, not from condensation.

Under section 11 of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985, the landlord is responsible for keeping the structure and exterior of the property in repair, and under the Homes (Fitness for Human Habitation) Act 2018, the property must be free from serious damp.

Please:
1. Arrange an inspection by a qualified surveyor or damp specialist by [date, about 14 days from now].
2. Confirm in writing what repairs will be carried out and when.
3. Pass this email to the landlord, and confirm that you have done so.

If I don't hear back by [date], I will contact [council name]'s private housing / environmental health team to request an inspection.

Kind regards,
[Your name]
[Phone number]

A few things that will strengthen your position:
- Photos with dates, ideally showing the patch over time and after rain.
- A cheap hygrometer showing indoor humidity. If it's under about 60% and the wall is still wet, that undercuts the condensation explanation.

- Ask for the landlord's name and address if you don't have it. You're entitled to it under section 1 of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985.

Very likely not done for. Starters are hard to kill.

The grey liquid is called **'hooch'**, an alcohol layer that forms when the yeast runs out of food. The **nail-polish-remover (acetone) smell** is a classic sign of a hungry starter, not a dead one. Both are normal after a month of neglect.

**To revive it:**
1. Pour off the hooch, or stir it in for a tangier flavour.
2. Discard most of the starter, keeping a tablespoon or two (about 20 to 50 g).
3. Feed it equal weights of flour and water, e.g. 50 g starter + 50 g flour + 50 g lukewarm water. Leave it at room temperature.
4. Repeat every 12 to 24 hours. After 2 to 4 feeds it should be bubbly, smell pleasantly sour and roughly double within 4 to 8 hours. Then it's ready to bake with.

**When to actually bin it:** pink, orange or red streaks, or fuzzy mould (white, green or black). In that case, start again rather than scraping.

Your pride is well placed, by the way. Surviving a month of neglect is a sign of a robust starter.

1. Give the last ten minutes a job. Plan a specific, brisk activity for that window that isn't the tail end of the main task: a quick quiz, a 'one thing I learned / one question' exit ticket that you collect at the door, a mini competition. 2. Make packing up a step you control. Build it in: 'At 2 minutes to, I'll say pack away.' Bags stay under desks until then. Equipment away, chairs in, exit ticket, then dismissal. Rehearse it like any other routine.

3. You dismiss, not the bell. Dismiss row by row or table by table, with the calmest/tidiest table going first. That creates a reason to sit down.

4. Use the exit ticket as the key to leave. Nobody leaves until they've handed it to you at the door. It also gives you useful data.

5. Friday-specific: consider front-loading the hardest content and keeping something engaging, like a practical demo or a short game, for the end. Make the end of the lesson something they don't want to miss.

6. When it slips, reset early. The week-long decay is normal. Re-teach the routine as soon as you see it slide, not after it's collapsed.

You're not doing anything awful, but there's a likely reason it's getting worse: if you go in after he's been crying for a while, he learns that crying for a long time eventually brings you. That's very strong reinforcement, and it builds longer crying, not less. Being consistent at that pattern makes it worse, not better.

At 10 weeks, though, he's a baby who has just left his litter and genuinely needs comfort, so the answer isn't to leave him to cry it out. It's to change when and how he gets you.

What tends to work:

1. Move the crate next to your bed for now. Being able to smell and hear you calms most puppies dramatically. You can rest a hand by the crate door. Move it out gradually over a few weeks once he's settling.

2. Respond early, not late. If he starts fussing, a calm low voice or your fingers at the door straight away, before it escalates, so he learns quiet gets him company.

3. Rule out real needs. At this age he probably needs a toilet trip once in the night. Do it boringly: out, wee, back in, no play.

4. Set him up to sleep. A good play and sniff session, then a calm wind-down, a last wee, and into the crate already drowsy. A chew, a snuggle toy or something that smells of you, and a cover over part of the crate can help.

5. Make the crate good in the daytime. Feed meals in it, give chews in it, and practise short calm periods in it while you're nearby, so it's not only the place where he's left alone at night.

Collies are sensitive and bright, so they learn patterns quickly, in both directions. Most puppies improve within a week or two with this setup. If he's still distressed after that, or seems panicked rather than just protesting, a qualified positive-reinforcement trainer or your vet is worth a call.
